problems.title: Flux through a tilted loop
problems.objective: Compute signed magnetic flux and distinguish the chosen surface normal from the physical loop.
problems.statement: A single rectangular loop has area $2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ in a uniform field of magnitude $0.30\,\mathrm T$. The field makes $60^\circ$ with the chosen positive unit normal. Find the signed magnetic flux. What changes if the opposite normal is chosen while the loop and field remain fixed?
problems.strategy: First: Use the angle between $\mathbf B$ and the chosen normal, not the plane of the loop. Next: For a uniform field and flat loop, reduce the integral to $BA\cos\theta$. Finally: Reverse only the oriented area vector when the normal is reversed.
hints: Use the angle between $\mathbf B$ and the chosen normal, not the plane of the loop.
For a uniform field and flat loop, reduce the integral to $BA\cos\theta$.
Reverse only the oriented area vector when the normal is reversed.
problems.solution: The flux is $\Phi_B=BA\cos60^\circ=(0.30)(2.0\times10^{-2})(1/2)=3.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}$. Choosing the opposite normal sends $d\mathbf A$ to $-d\mathbf A$, so the signed flux becomes $-3.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}$. No physical field or loop property changes; only the orientation convention changes.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use the angle between $\mathbf B$ and the chosen normal, not the plane of the loop.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For a uniform field and flat loop, reduce the integral to $BA\cos\theta$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Reverse only the oriented area vector when the normal is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $BA\sin60^\circ$ because $60^\circ$ is treated as an angle from the loop plane.
commonErrors.consequence: The projection is taken with respect to the wrong geometric direction.

commonErrors.description: Claims reversing the normal reverses the magnetic field.
commonErrors.consequence: A bookkeeping orientation is confused with a physical change of the source.

problems.flawedProof: The flux is $BA\sin60^\circ$, and reversing the normal reverses $\mathbf B$, so the flux keeps the same sign.

problems.title: Lenz direction for an increasing inward field
problems.objective: Determine induced-current direction from a signed flux change.
problems.statement: A circular conducting loop of radius $0.10\,\mathrm m$ lies in the page. A uniform magnetic field into the page increases at $0.50\,\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$. Take the positive loop normal out of the page. Find the induced emf and state whether the induced current is clockwise or counterclockwise.
problems.strategy: First: With the positive normal out of the page, the applied flux is negative and becoming more negative. Next: Use $A=\pi r^2$ to obtain the signed emf. Finally: Relate the sign of $\mathcal E$ to the positive circulation direction set by the chosen normal.
hints: With the positive normal out of the page, the applied flux is negative and becoming more negative.
Use $A=\pi r^2$ to obtain the signed emf.
Relate the sign of $\mathcal E$ to the positive circulation direction set by the chosen normal.
problems.solution: The applied flux is $\Phi_B=-B\pi r^2$, so $d\Phi_B/dt=-(0.50)\pi(0.10)^2\,\mathrm{Wb\,s^{-1}}$. Hence $\mathcal E=-d\Phi_B/dt=+1.57\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm V$. Positive circulation for an outward normal is counterclockwise. The induced field therefore points out of the page and opposes the increasing inward flux.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: With the positive normal out of the page, the applied flux is negative and becoming more negative.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $A=\pi r^2$ to obtain the signed emf.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Relate the sign of $\mathcal E$ to the positive circulation direction set by the chosen normal.

commonErrors.description: Says the induced current reinforces the increasing inward field.
commonErrors.consequence: The response violates Lenz's law and would create energy without an external source.

commonErrors.description: Uses the loop circumference in place of its area when computing flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The result has incorrect dimensions and magnitude.

problems.flawedProof: The field points inward, so the loop should make more inward field. Using $2\pi r$ gives $\mathcal E=0.314\,\mathrm V$ clockwise.

problems.title: Motional emf and the positive rod end
problems.objective: Calculate motional emf and determine charge separation using the magnetic force.
problems.statement: A conducting rod of length $0.40\,\mathrm m$ is vertical and moves right at $3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ through a uniform $0.50\,\mathrm T$ field into the page. Find the open-circuit potential difference and identify which end of the rod is at higher potential.
problems.strategy: First: Evaluate $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ for a positive test charge. Next: The magnitude is $B\ell v$ because the three directions are mutually perpendicular. Finally: The end toward which positive charge is pushed is at higher potential.
hints: Evaluate $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ for a positive test charge.
The magnitude is $B\ell v$ because the three directions are mutually perpendicular.
The end toward which positive charge is pushed is at higher potential.
problems.solution: Here $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=\mathbf e_x\times(-\mathbf e_z)=+\mathbf e_y$, so positive charge is driven upward. The top is at higher potential, and $V_{\rm top}-V_{\rm bottom}=B\ell v=(0.50)(0.40)(3.0)=0.60\,\mathrm V$. The units $\mathrm{T\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$ reduce to volts.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Evaluate $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ for a positive test charge.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The magnitude is $B\ell v$ because the three directions are mutually perpendicular.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The end toward which positive charge is pushed is at higher potential.

commonErrors.description: Applies the right-hand rule as though the mobile positive charges move left.
commonErrors.consequence: The rod polarity is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $Bv/\ell$ for the emf.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression has the wrong dimensions and decreases with rod length.

problems.flawedProof: The magnetic force points down, so the bottom is positive. The voltage is $Bv/\ell=3.75\,\mathrm V$.

problems.title: A loop entering and then crossing a uniform field
problems.objective: Identify when changing overlap area produces emf and when rigid translation does not.
problems.statement: A rectangular loop moves right at constant speed into a region with a uniform magnetic field into the page. Describe the induced-current direction while the leading edge enters, while the loop is completely inside, and while the trailing edge exits. Assume the field region is wider than the loop.
problems.strategy: First: Track the overlap area between the loop and field region during each stage. Next: An increasing inward flux requires an outward induced field; constant flux gives zero emf. Finally: When the loop exits, the inward flux decreases and the induced direction reverses.
hints: Track the overlap area between the loop and field region during each stage.
An increasing inward flux requires an outward induced field; constant flux gives zero emf.
When the loop exits, the inward flux decreases and the induced direction reverses.
problems.solution: During entry the inward flux magnitude increases, so the loop produces an outward field and carries counterclockwise current. Once fully inside, the loop encloses constant uniform flux, so $d\Phi_B/dt=0$ and there is no induced current. During exit the inward flux decreases, so the loop attempts to preserve it and the current is clockwise. The result depends on flux change, not merely on motion through a field.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Track the overlap area between the loop and field region during each stage.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: An increasing inward flux requires an outward induced field; constant flux gives zero emf.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: When the loop exits, the inward flux decreases and the induced direction reverses.

commonErrors.description: Claims any loop moving through a magnetic field must carry induced current.
commonErrors.consequence: Rigid translation inside a spatially uniform field is mistaken for a flux change.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same current direction during entry and exit.
commonErrors.consequence: The opposite signs of the two flux changes are ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The loop is always moving, so it carries counterclockwise current at every stage, including while fully inside and while exiting.

problems.title: Inductor energy from current
problems.objective: Compute stored magnetic energy and distinguish inductance from resistance.
problems.statement: An ideal $0.20\,\mathrm H$ inductor carries $3.0\,\mathrm A$. Find its stored magnetic energy. If the current is momentarily constant, what is the inductor voltage under the passive sign convention?
problems.strategy: First: Insert the current, not a current derivative, into the energy formula. Next: For a momentarily constant current, evaluate $dI/dt$. Finally: Check that henry times ampere squared is a joule.
hints: Insert the current, not a current derivative, into the energy formula.
For a momentarily constant current, evaluate $dI/dt$.
Check that henry times ampere squared is a joule.
problems.solution: The stored energy is $U_L=\tfrac12(0.20)(3.0)^2=0.90\,\mathrm J$. A momentarily constant current has $dI/dt=0$, so $v_L=0$ even though the magnetic energy is nonzero. This is analogous to a charged capacitor that may store energy while its current is zero.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Insert the current, not a current derivative, into the energy formula.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For a momentarily constant current, evaluate $dI/dt$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check that henry times ampere squared is a joule.

commonErrors.description: Uses $LI/2$ instead of $LI^2/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The value and dimensions are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims nonzero stored energy requires a nonzero inductor voltage.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy storage is confused with the instantaneous rate of current change.

problems.flawedProof: The energy is $LI/2=0.30\,\mathrm J$. Since the inductor stores energy, its voltage must also be nonzero.

problems.title: Read an RL time constant
problems.objective: Calculate the characteristic response time of a series resistor-inductor circuit.
problems.statement: A $0.60\,\mathrm H$ ideal inductor is in series with a $12\,\Omega$ resistor. Find the RL time constant and the fraction of a decaying current that remains after one time constant.
problems.strategy: First: Use $L/R$, not $R/L$, for the quantity with units of time. Next: Set $t=\tau$ in the decay factor. Finally: Report both seconds and the dimensionless remaining fraction.
hints: Use $L/R$, not $R/L$, for the quantity with units of time.
Set $t=\tau$ in the decay factor.
Report both seconds and the dimensionless remaining fraction.
problems.solution: The time constant is $\tau=L/R=0.60/12=5.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm s$. At $t=\tau$, $I/I_0=e^{-1}\approx0.368$, so about $36.8\%$ remains. Since $\mathrm H/\Omega=\mathrm s$, the units check.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $L/R$, not $R/L$, for the quantity with units of time.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Set $t=\tau$ in the decay factor.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Report both seconds and the dimensionless remaining fraction.

commonErrors.description: Uses $R/L=20$ as a time in seconds.
commonErrors.consequence: The decay rate is mistaken for the time constant.

commonErrors.description: Says one time constant means the current has reached exactly zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Exponential decay is incorrectly treated as finite-time extinction.

problems.flawedProof: The time constant is $R/L=20\,\mathrm s$, and after that time the current is zero.

problems.title: Ideal transformer voltage and current ratios
problems.objective: Apply ideal transformer ratios while preserving input-output power.
problems.statement: An ideal transformer has $N_p=500$ primary turns and $N_s=100$ secondary turns. The primary is driven at $120\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. Find the secondary rms voltage. If the secondary supplies $2.0\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$, find the primary rms current.
problems.strategy: First: The secondary has one fifth as many turns as the primary. Next: Use the inverse turns ratio for current or conserve ideal power. Finally: Confirm that input and output apparent powers agree.
hints: The secondary has one fifth as many turns as the primary.
Use the inverse turns ratio for current or conserve ideal power.
Confirm that input and output apparent powers agree.
problems.solution: The voltage is $V_s=120(100/500)=24\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. Power conservation gives $I_p=V_sI_s/V_p=(24)(2.0)/120=0.40\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$. Both sides carry $48\,\mathrm{VA}$, as required by the ideal model.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The secondary has one fifth as many turns as the primary.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use the inverse turns ratio for current or conserve ideal power.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Confirm that input and output apparent powers agree.

commonErrors.description: Uses the primary-to-secondary turns ratio and predicts a 600 V secondary.
commonErrors.consequence: The step-down transformer is treated as a step-up transformer.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same turns ratio for voltage and current.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed powers on the two sides do not match.

problems.flawedProof: The secondary voltage is $120(500/100)=600\,\mathrm V$, and its $2.0\,\mathrm A$ current implies a $10\,\mathrm A$ primary current.

problems.title: A decreasing outward field
problems.objective: Combine a field derivative with loop area and a Lenz-law direction.
problems.statement: A square loop of side $0.20\,\mathrm m$ lies in a magnetic field directed out of the page. The field decreases uniformly at $0.40\,\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$. Find the emf magnitude and induced-current direction.
problems.strategy: First: The loop area is the square of its side. Next: A decreasing outward flux is opposed by an induced outward field. Finally: Use the right-hand rule to convert the induced field into current direction.
hints: The loop area is the square of its side.
A decreasing outward flux is opposed by an induced outward field.
Use the right-hand rule to convert the induced field into current direction.
problems.solution: The magnitude is $|\mathcal E|=a^2|dB/dt|=(0.20)^2(0.40)=1.6\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm V$. To oppose the loss of outward flux, the induced field points out of the page. The induced current is therefore counterclockwise.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The loop area is the square of its side.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: A decreasing outward flux is opposed by an induced outward field.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the right-hand rule to convert the induced field into current direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses side length rather than area in the flux derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The emf is numerically and dimensionally wrong.

commonErrors.description: Chooses an inward induced field because the applied field is outward.
commonErrors.consequence: Lenz's law is applied to field direction instead of flux change.

problems.flawedProof: The emf is $a|dB/dt|=0.080\,\mathrm V$. Because the applied field is outward, the induced field must be inward and the current clockwise.

problems.title: Sliding rod power balance
problems.objective: Relate motional emf, magnetic drag, mechanical power, and Joule heating.
problems.statement: A rod of length $0.50\,\mathrm m$ slides at constant $2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ on conducting rails in a uniform perpendicular field $0.80\,\mathrm T$. The complete circuit resistance is $4.0\,\Omega$ and self-inductance is negligible. Find the emf, current magnitude, magnetic drag force, and external mechanical power required.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the motional emf before applying Ohm's law. Next: The magnetic force opposes the maintained motion by Lenz's law. Finally: Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$.
hints: Compute the motional emf before applying Ohm's law.
The magnetic force opposes the maintained motion by Lenz's law.
Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$.
problems.solution: The emf is $\mathcal E=(0.80)(0.50)(2.0)=0.80\,\mathrm V$, so $I=0.80/4.0=0.20\,\mathrm A$. The magnetic drag has magnitude $F=I\ell B=(0.20)(0.50)(0.80)=0.080\,\mathrm N$. Constant speed requires an equal external force in the direction of motion, so $P_{\rm ext}=Fv=0.160\,\mathrm W$. The circuit dissipates $I^2R=(0.20)^2(4.0)=0.160\,\mathrm W$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Compute the motional emf before applying Ohm's law.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The magnetic force opposes the maintained motion by Lenz's law.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$.

commonErrors.description: Places the magnetic force in the direction of motion.
commonErrors.consequence: The result violates Lenz's law and the energy balance.

commonErrors.description: Equates mechanical power to $IR$ rather than $I^2R$.
commonErrors.consequence: A voltage is mistaken for power.

problems.flawedProof: The field assists the rod, so $F=0.080\,\mathrm N$ forward. The required power is $IR=0.80\,\mathrm W$.

problems.title: Peak emf of a rotating coil
problems.objective: Derive the sinusoidal emf amplitude of a rigid coil rotating in a uniform field.
problems.statement: A coil with $200$ turns and area $1.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at $100\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ in a uniform $0.50\,\mathrm T$ field. Its area normal is parallel to the field at $t=0$. Write the flux linkage and emf as functions of time, and find the peak emf.
problems.strategy: First: The angle between the field and coil normal is $\omega t$. Next: Differentiate $NBA\cos(\omega t)$ with its sign. Finally: The peak is the coefficient of the sine function.
hints: The angle between the field and coil normal is $\omega t$.
Differentiate $NBA\cos(\omega t)$ with its sign.
The peak is the coefficient of the sine function.
problems.solution: The flux linkage is $N\Phi_B=NBA\cos(\omega t)$. Therefore $\mathcal E(t)=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$ for the circulation convention consistent with the chosen normal. The peak value is $NBA\omega=(200)(0.50)(1.0\times10^{-2})(100)=100\,\mathrm V$. At $t=0$ the flux is maximal and the emf is zero, a useful phase check.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The angle between the field and coil normal is $\omega t$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate $NBA\cos(\omega t)$ with its sign.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The peak is the coefficient of the sine function.

commonErrors.description: Omits the number of turns from the flux linkage.
commonErrors.consequence: The emf is underestimated by a factor of 200.

commonErrors.description: Writes maximum emf at the instant of maximum flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative-phase relation is lost.

problems.flawedProof: The emf is $BA\omega\cos(\omega t)$, so it peaks at $t=0$ with value $0.50\,\mathrm V$.

problems.title: Flux of a radially varying field
problems.objective: Integrate a nonuniform magnetic field over a circular surface with the correct Jacobian.
problems.statement: A circular loop of radius $R$ lies perpendicular to $\mathbf e_z$. Over its surface, $\mathbf B(r)=B_0(1-r^2/R^2)\mathbf e_z$. Using the $+\mathbf e_z$ normal, compute the magnetic flux.
problems.strategy: First: Do not replace the varying field by its central value. Next: Integrate $B_0(1-r^2/R^2)r$ from $0$ to $R$ and $\phi$ from $0$ to $2\pi$. Finally: Compare the result with $B_0\pi R^2$ to check that it is smaller than the uniform-central-field flux.
hints: Do not replace the varying field by its central value.
Integrate $B_0(1-r^2/R^2)r$ from $0$ to $R$ and $\phi$ from $0$ to $2\pi$.
Compare the result with $B_0\pi R^2$ to check that it is smaller than the uniform-central-field flux.
problems.solution:
The flux is
$\Phi_B=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R B_0(1-r^2/R^2)r\,dr\,d\phi
=2\pi B_0[R^2/2-R^2/4]=\pi B_0R^2/2$.
It is half the flux that a uniform field $B_0$ would produce, consistent with the field decreasing to zero at the rim.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Do not replace the varying field by its central value.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Integrate $B_0(1-r^2/R^2)r$ from $0$ to $R$ and $\phi$ from $0$ to $2\pi$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare the result with $B_0\pi R^2$ to check that it is smaller than the uniform-central-field flux.

commonErrors.description: Uses $B_0\pi R^2$ without integrating the spatial variation.
commonErrors.consequence: The field is treated as uniform at its maximum value.

commonErrors.description: Omits the radial Jacobian factor in the area element.
commonErrors.consequence: The integral has the wrong radial weighting and dimensions.

problems.flawedProof: The field is $B_0$ at the center, so the flux is simply $B_0\pi R^2$.

problems.title: Mutual induction from a current ramp
problems.objective: Compute a mutual-induction emf and interpret its polarity through Lenz's law.
problems.statement: Two stationary coils have mutual inductance $M=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm H$ under a stated dot convention. The current entering the dotted terminal of coil 1 increases at $50\,\mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}$. Find the magnitude of the open-circuit emf in coil 2 and state the polarity relation needed to oppose the increasing linked flux.
permittedResults: $v_2=\pm M\,di_1/dt$, with the sign fixed by the declared terminal convention.
problems.strategy: First: Use the mutual inductance and the current slope for the magnitude. Next: The numerical magnitude is independent of how the voltage reference is labeled. Finally: Use the dot convention and Lenz's law together to state which referenced terminal is positive.
hints: Use the mutual inductance and the current slope for the magnitude.
The numerical magnitude is independent of how the voltage reference is labeled.
Use the dot convention and Lenz's law together to state which referenced terminal is positive.
problems.solution: The magnitude is $|v_2|=M|di_1/dt|=(2.0\times10^{-2})(50)=1.0\,\mathrm V$. For the usual coupled-inductor convention, currents entering both dotted terminals contribute positive mutual flux; the induced open-circuit voltage must have the polarity that would drive a current opposing the increase. A numerical sign cannot be stated without the diagram's voltage-reference arrows, but the opposition rule is invariant.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use the mutual inductance and the current slope for the magnitude.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The numerical magnitude is independent of how the voltage reference is labeled.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the dot convention and Lenz's law together to state which referenced terminal is positive.

commonErrors.description: Uses $Mi_1$ rather than $M\,di_1/dt$ as a voltage.
commonErrors.consequence: Flux linkage is confused with induced emf.

commonErrors.description: Declares a terminal positive without consulting the stated dot and voltage conventions.
commonErrors.consequence: A convention-dependent sign is asserted from incomplete data.

problems.flawedProof: The secondary voltage is $Mi_1$, and the dotted terminal is always positive regardless of the reference arrows.

problems.title: Self-inductance of a long solenoid
problems.objective: Derive and evaluate solenoid inductance from flux linkage.
problems.statement: An air-core solenoid has $N=500$ turns, length $0.50\,\mathrm m$, and cross-sectional area $4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Neglect fringing. Derive its self-inductance and evaluate it numerically.
problems.strategy: First: Find the flux through one turn and then multiply by all $N$ turns. Next: Set $N\Phi_B=LI$ and cancel the current. Finally: Check the scaling with $N^2$, area, and inverse length.
hints: Find the flux through one turn and then multiply by all $N$ turns.
Set $N\Phi_B=LI$ and cancel the current.
Check the scaling with $N^2$, area, and inverse length.
problems.solution:
One turn has flux $\Phi_B=BA=\mu_0(N/\ell)IA$. Thus $N\Phi_B=\mu_0N^2AI/\ell$, so $L=\mu_0N^2A/\ell$. Numerically,
$L=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(500)^2(4.0\times10^{-4})/0.50
=2.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm H$.
The $N^2$ dependence reflects that turns both create and link the field.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Find the flux through one turn and then multiply by all $N$ turns.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Set $N\Phi_B=LI$ and cancel the current.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check the scaling with $N^2$, area, and inverse length.

commonErrors.description: Includes only one factor of the turn count.
commonErrors.consequence: The flux created by all turns or the linkage of all turns is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Places solenoid length in the numerator.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted inductance increases when turn density decreases.

problems.flawedProof: Since one turn has flux $BA$, the inductance is $L=\mu_0NA\ell$, with only one factor of $N$.

problems.title: Current growth after closing an RL switch
problems.objective: Solve a first-order RL step response and evaluate it at one time constant.
problems.statement: A $12\,\mathrm V$ ideal source, $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor, and $3.0\,\mathrm H$ inductor are placed in series at $t=0$ with initial current zero. Find $I(t)$, the time constant, and the current at one time constant.
permittedResults: Kirchhoff's loop rule and the ideal inductor law.
problems.strategy: First: Write $L\,dI/dt+RI=V$ and identify the long-time current. Next: Use $I(0)=0$ to fix the exponential coefficient. Finally: At $t=\tau$, use $1-e^{-1}$.
hints: Write $L\,dI/dt+RI=V$ and identify the long-time current.
Use $I(0)=0$ to fix the exponential coefficient.
At $t=\tau$, use $1-e^{-1}$.
problems.solution: The loop equation is $3\,dI/dt+6I=12$. Its steady current is $V/R=2.0\,\mathrm A$ and $\tau=L/R=0.50\,\mathrm s$, so $I(t)=2.0(1-e^{-t/0.50})\,\mathrm A$. At one time constant, $I=2.0(1-e^{-1})=1.26\,\mathrm A$. The current is continuous at switching and tends to $2.0\,\mathrm A$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Write $L\,dI/dt+RI=V$ and identify the long-time current.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $I(0)=0$ to fix the exponential coefficient.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: At $t=\tau$, use $1-e^{-1}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses an exponentially decaying current from zero for a source turn-on.
commonErrors.consequence: The initial condition and steady state are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses $R/L$ as the time constant.
commonErrors.consequence: A decay rate is inserted where a time is required.

problems.flawedProof: The current is $I(t)=2e^{-2t}\,\mathrm A$, because every inductor transient decays from the final current.

problems.title: Source-free RL decay
problems.objective: Apply inductor-current continuity to a discharge transient.
problems.statement: A $2.0\,\mathrm H$ inductor initially carries $4.0\,\mathrm A$. At $t=0$ it is connected across a $10\,\Omega$ resistor with no source. Find the current and resistor power at $t=0.40\,\mathrm s$.
problems.strategy: First: The inductor current immediately after switching remains $4.0\,\mathrm A$. Next: Compute $t/\tau$ with $\tau=L/R$. Finally: Use $P_R=I^2R$ after finding the current.
hints: The inductor current immediately after switching remains $4.0\,\mathrm A$.
Compute $t/\tau$ with $\tau=L/R$.
Use $P_R=I^2R$ after finding the current.
problems.solution: The time constant is $\tau=2.0/10=0.20\,\mathrm s$, so at $0.40\,\mathrm s=2\tau$, $I=4.0e^{-2}=0.541\,\mathrm A$. The resistor power is $P_R=I^2R=(0.541)^2(10)=2.93\,\mathrm W$. The power is positive dissipation while the inductor's stored energy decreases.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The inductor current immediately after switching remains $4.0\,\mathrm A$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Compute $t/\tau$ with $\tau=L/R$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use $P_R=I^2R$ after finding the current.

commonErrors.description: Sets the current instantly to zero when the source is absent.
commonErrors.consequence: Inductor-current continuity is violated and would require infinite voltage.

commonErrors.description: Uses $IR$ as resistor power.
commonErrors.consequence: Voltage is reported instead of power.

problems.flawedProof: Removing the source makes $I(0^+)=0$, so the resistor power is also zero for all later times.

problems.title: Field energy inside a solenoid
problems.objective: Reconcile field-energy density with the lumped inductor formula.
problems.statement: A long air-core solenoid has turn density $n=1000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, cross-sectional area $2.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, length $0.40\,\mathrm m$, and current $2.0\,\mathrm A$. Neglect fringing. Find its magnetic field, field-energy density, and total stored energy. Verify the result using $L=\mu_0n^2A\ell$.
problems.strategy: First: Use the long-solenoid field only inside the modeled volume $A\ell$. Next: Multiply the energy density by $A\ell$. Finally: Compute the inductance independently and compare $LI^2/2$.
hints: Use the long-solenoid field only inside the modeled volume $A\ell$.
Multiply the energy density by $A\ell$.
Compute the inductance independently and compare $LI^2/2$.
problems.solution: The field is $B=\mu_0nI=2.51\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm T$. Thus $u_B=B^2/(2\mu_0)=2.51\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The modeled field volume is $A\ell=8.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^3}$, giving $U=2.01\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$. Also $L=\mu_0n^2A\ell=1.01\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm H$, so $LI^2/2=2.01\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use the long-solenoid field only inside the modeled volume $A\ell$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Multiply the energy density by $A\ell$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compute the inductance independently and compare $LI^2/2$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $B^2/\mu_0$ without the factor $1/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The stored energy is doubled.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies energy density by solenoid length but not cross-sectional area.
commonErrors.consequence: A density is not integrated over volume and the units remain wrong.

problems.flawedProof: The energy density is $B^2/\mu_0$, and total energy is this density times $\ell$, giving a result in joules.

problems.title: Natural frequency of an LC oscillator

problems.statement: An ideal LC circuit has $L=20\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $C=5.0\,\mu\mathrm F$. Find its natural angular frequency and frequency in hertz.
problems.strategy: First: Convert millihenries and microfarads to SI units before multiplying. Next: Take the reciprocal square root to obtain radians per second. Finally: Divide by $2\pi$ only when converting to hertz.
hints: Convert millihenries and microfarads to SI units before multiplying.
Take the reciprocal square root to obtain radians per second.
Divide by $2\pi$ only when converting to hertz.
problems.solution: Here $LC=(20\times10^{-3})(5.0\times10^{-6})=1.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s^2}$. Therefore $\omega_0=3.16\times10^3\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $f_0=\omega_0/(2\pi)=5.03\times10^2\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Convert millihenries and microfarads to SI units before multiplying.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Take the reciprocal square root to obtain radians per second.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Divide by $2\pi$ only when converting to hertz.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the printed milli and micro values without converting prefixes.
commonErrors.consequence: The frequency is wrong by orders of magnitude.

commonErrors.description: Reports angular frequency directly in hertz.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor of $2\pi$ between angular and cyclic frequency is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Since $LC=100$, the frequency is $1/\sqrt{100}=0.10\,\mathrm{Hz}$, which is also the angular frequency.

problems.title: Series RLC resonance and average power
problems.objective: Find resonance and the current-power response of a driven series RLC circuit.
problems.statement: A series circuit has $R=6.0\,\Omega$, $L=0.10\,\mathrm H$, and $C=10\,\mu\mathrm F$. It is driven by a sinusoidal source with $12\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. Find the resonant angular frequency, rms current at resonance, and average power absorbed.
permittedResults: At series resonance, $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$ and the impedance is $R$.
problems.strategy: First: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel. Next: Use rms voltage with rms current. Finally: Only the resistor absorbs net average power in the ideal model.
hints: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.
Use rms voltage with rms current.
Only the resistor absorbs net average power in the ideal model.
problems.solution: The resonance is $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{(0.10)(10\times10^{-6})}=1.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. At resonance $Z=R=6.0\,\Omega$, so $I_{\rm rms}=12/6.0=2.0\,\mathrm A$. The average absorbed power is $I_{\rm rms}^2R=(2.0)^2(6.0)=24\,\mathrm W$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use rms voltage with rms current.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Only the resistor absorbs net average power in the ideal model.

commonErrors.description: Adds inductive and capacitive reactance magnitudes at resonance.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining cancellation at resonance is missed.

commonErrors.description: Combines rms voltage with peak-current formulas.
commonErrors.consequence: The power acquires an erroneous factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: At resonance the reactances add, so $Z=R+2\omega_0L$ and the current is much smaller than $2.0\,\mathrm A$.

problems.title: Load current reflected through a transformer
problems.objective: Use ideal transformer power and turns ratios for a loaded device.
problems.statement: An ideal transformer has turns ratio $N_p:N_s=10:1$ and is connected to $240\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$ on the primary. A resistive load absorbs $120\,\mathrm W$ from the secondary. Find the secondary voltage, secondary current, and primary current.
permittedResults: Ideal transformer voltage ratio and power conservation.
problems.strategy: First: Use the turns ratio to find the secondary voltage. Next: For the resistive load, use $P=V_sI_s$. Finally: Conserve power to find the primary current.
hints: Use the turns ratio to find the secondary voltage.
For the resistive load, use $P=V_sI_s$.
Conserve power to find the primary current.
problems.solution: The secondary voltage is $V_s=240/10=24\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. The load current is $I_s=P/V_s=120/24=5.0\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$. Ideal input power also equals $120\,\mathrm W$, so $I_p=120/240=0.50\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$. The current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use the turns ratio to find the secondary voltage.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For the resistive load, use $P=V_sI_s$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Conserve power to find the primary current.

commonErrors.description: Uses 240 V as the secondary voltage.
commonErrors.consequence: The turns ratio is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Sets primary and secondary currents equal.
commonErrors.consequence: Input and output powers differ by a factor of ten.

problems.flawedProof: An ideal transformer has the same voltage and current on both sides, so $V_s=240\,\mathrm V$ and $I_p=I_s=0.50\,\mathrm A$.

problems.title: Why eddy-current braking cannot speed a plate
problems.objective: Explain magnetic braking through Lenz's law and an energy audit.
problems.statement: A conducting plate moves into a localized magnetic-field region with no mechanical contact. It slows and warms. Explain the direction of the induced currents and magnetic force, identify the energy source for the heating, and predict what happens if narrow insulating slots are cut parallel to the plate's motion.
permittedResults: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, and Joule heating.
problems.strategy: First: The moving plate samples a changing magnetic flux through possible current loops. Next: The induced force must oppose the flux-changing motion when no other energy source is present. Finally: Slots interrupt large circulating-current paths and raise their effective resistance.
hints: The moving plate samples a changing magnetic flux through possible current loops.
The induced force must oppose the flux-changing motion when no other energy source is present.
Slots interrupt large circulating-current paths and raise their effective resistance.
problems.solution: As portions of the plate enter and leave the field, eddy currents circulate so that their magnetic field opposes each local flux change. Their interaction with the applied field produces a net drag force. The lost translational kinetic energy becomes primarily Joule heat in the plate; the magnetic field does no net free work without its source participating. Slots break large loops into smaller, more resistive paths, reducing eddy-current magnitude, drag, and heating.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The moving plate samples a changing magnetic flux through possible current loops.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The induced force must oppose the flux-changing motion when no other energy source is present.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Slots interrupt large circulating-current paths and raise their effective resistance.

commonErrors.description: Claims the magnetic field supplies the heat while the plate's kinetic energy stays fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy conservation is violated in the stated passive setup.

commonErrors.description: Predicts slots strengthen braking by exposing more edge area.
commonErrors.consequence: The dominant effect of interrupting circulating current paths is missed.

problems.flawedProof: The magnetic field adds energy to the plate and the eddy currents push it forward. Cutting slots creates more edges, so the forward push becomes stronger.

problems.title: Induced electric field around a changing solenoid field
problems.objective: Derive the azimuthal electric field inside and outside a circular changing-field region.
problems.statement: A very long solenoid produces a uniform axial field $B(t)$ for $r<R$ and negligible field for $r>R$. By symmetry the induced electric field is azimuthal. Derive $E_\phi(r,t)$ for $r<R$ and $r>R$, using counterclockwise circulation as positive when $B$ points in $+z$.
problems.strategy: First: Use a circular integration path and distinguish whether its radius lies inside or outside $R$. Next: For $r<R$, the enclosed changing area is $\pi r^2$; for $r>R$, it is $\pi R^2$. Finally: Divide the signed circulation by $2\pi r$ and check continuity at $r=R$.
hints: Use a circular integration path and distinguish whether its radius lies inside or outside $R$.
For $r<R$, the enclosed changing area is $\pi r^2$; for $r>R$, it is $\pi R^2$.
Divide the signed circulation by $2\pi r$ and check continuity at $r=R$.
problems.solution: Symmetry makes $E_\phi$ constant on a circle. For $r<R$, $2\pi rE_\phi=-\pi r^2\dot B$, hence $E_\phi=-(r/2)\dot B$. For $r>R$, only the solenoid cross-section contributes: $2\pi rE_\phi=-\pi R^2\dot B$, so $E_\phi=-(R^2/2r)\dot B$. Both give $-(R/2)\dot B$ at the boundary. The field outside is nonzero even where the modeled magnetic field is negligible.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use a circular integration path and distinguish whether its radius lies inside or outside $R$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For $r<R$, the enclosed changing area is $\pi r^2$; for $r>R$, it is $\pi R^2$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Divide the signed circulation by $2\pi r$ and check continuity at $r=R$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the path's full area for exterior circles even though the magnetic field is confined to the solenoid.
commonErrors.consequence: The exterior electric field incorrectly grows with radius.

commonErrors.description: Sets the exterior electric field to zero because the local magnetic field is zero there.
commonErrors.consequence: Faraday's law is treated as a pointwise local proportionality.

problems.flawedProof: Outside the solenoid $B=0$, so $E_\phi=0$. Inside, using flux $B\pi R^2$ for every path gives $E_\phi=-R^2\dot B/(2r)$.

problems.title: RMS emf of a laboratory generator
problems.objective: Convert rotational frequency into angular speed and rms generator voltage.
problems.statement: A $100$-turn coil of area $2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ in a uniform $0.50\,\mathrm T$ field. Find the peak and rms induced emf for sinusoidal rotation.
problems.strategy: First: Convert $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $\omega=2\pi f$. Next: Multiply by the turn count, field, area, and angular speed. Finally: Use the sinusoidal rms factor only after finding the peak.
hints: Convert $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $\omega=2\pi f$.
Multiply by the turn count, field, area, and angular speed.
Use the sinusoidal rms factor only after finding the peak.
problems.solution: The angular speed is $\omega=2\pi(60)=377\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Thus $\mathcal E_{\max}=(100)(0.50)(2.0\times10^{-2})(377)=377\,\mathrm V$. The rms value is $377/\sqrt2=267\,\mathrm V$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Convert $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $\omega=2\pi f$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Multiply by the turn count, field, area, and angular speed.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the sinusoidal rms factor only after finding the peak.

commonErrors.description: Uses 60 directly as an angular speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The result is too small by a factor of $2\pi$.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the peak by $\sqrt2$ to obtain rms voltage.
commonErrors.consequence: The peak-rms relation is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: The angular speed is $60\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so the peak is $60\,\mathrm V$ and the rms value is $60\sqrt2\,\mathrm V$.

problems.title: Mechanical work while a loop enters a field
problems.objective: Derive entry-stage drag and reconcile mechanical work with Joule heat.
problems.statement: A rectangular loop of resistance $3.0\,\Omega$ has side length $0.30\,\mathrm m$ perpendicular to its velocity. It enters a uniform $0.50\,\mathrm T$ field at constant $2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Neglect self-inductance and edge fringing. During entry, find the emf, current, magnetic drag, and external power. Explain why no drag remains once the loop is fully inside the uniform field.
permittedResults: Faraday's law, Ohm's law, and magnetic force on a straight segment.
problems.strategy: First: During entry, the overlap area grows at rate $\ell v$. Next: Only the leading segment has an uncompensated horizontal magnetic force. Finally: Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$, then set $d\Phi_B/dt=0$ when fully inside.
hints: During entry, the overlap area grows at rate $\ell v$.
Only the leading segment has an uncompensated horizontal magnetic force.
Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$, then set $d\Phi_B/dt=0$ when fully inside.
problems.solution: During entry, $|\mathcal E|=B\ell v=(0.50)(0.30)(2.0)=0.30\,\mathrm V$, so $I=0.10\,\mathrm A$. The drag is $F=I\ell B=(0.10)(0.30)(0.50)=1.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm N$. Maintaining speed requires $P=Fv=3.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm W$, equal to $I^2R=(0.10)^2(3.0)$. Once fully inside, the flux is constant; currents vanish and forces on opposite sides would cancel.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: During entry, the overlap area grows at rate $\ell v$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Only the leading segment has an uncompensated horizontal magnetic force.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare $Fv$ with $I^2R$, then set $d\Phi_B/dt=0$ when fully inside.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full loop perimeter as the area-growth rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The motional emf is overcounted.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the same current after the loop is fully inside a uniform field.
commonErrors.consequence: A constant-flux stage is treated as though flux were changing.

problems.flawedProof: The area changes at the perimeter times speed, so all four sides contribute the same emf. The current and drag continue unchanged after the loop is fully inside.

problems.title: A small loop moving through a field gradient
problems.objective: Differentiate spatially varying flux along a prescribed trajectory.
problems.statement: A small rigid loop of area $A=1.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ has fixed normal $+\mathbf e_z$ and moves in $+x$ at $3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Over the loop, the field is approximately uniform but varies as $\mathbf B(x)=(B_0+kx)\mathbf e_z$ with $k=0.20\,\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$. Find the signed emf for counterclockwise positive circulation. State the approximation being used.
problems.strategy: First: Under the small-loop approximation, use $\Phi_B\approx AB(x)$. Next: Apply the chain rule $dB/dt=(dB/dx)v$. Finally: Keep the sign associated with the chosen normal and circulation.
hints: Under the small-loop approximation, use $\Phi_B\approx AB(x)$.
Apply the chain rule $dB/dt=(dB/dx)v$.
Keep the sign associated with the chosen normal and circulation.
problems.solution: The approximate flux is $\Phi_B=A(B_0+kx)$, so $d\Phi_B/dt=Ak v$. Therefore $\mathcal E=-Akv=-(1.0\times10^{-2})(0.20)(3.0)=-6.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm V$. The approximation assumes the field variation across the loop is negligible relative to its value at the loop's representative position.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Under the small-loop approximation, use $\Phi_B\approx AB(x)$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Apply the chain rule $dB/dt=(dB/dx)v$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Keep the sign associated with the chosen normal and circulation.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates with respect to $x$ but omits $dx/dt$.
commonErrors.consequence: The result has units of volts per speed rather than volts.

commonErrors.description: Treats the field as exactly uniform in all space and predicts zero emf.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated spatial gradient is discarded.

problems.flawedProof: Because the loop is rigid and the field is time independent, $d\Phi_B/dt=0$. Motion through a static field can never produce emf.

problems.title: A square loop beside a time-varying long-wire current
problems.objective: Integrate nonuniform linked flux and differentiate the source current.
problems.statement: A square loop of side $a$ lies in the plane of a very long straight wire. Its nearer edge is distance $x$ from the wire, and the wire current $I(t)$ is increasing. Derive the magnetic flux through the loop and the induced emf magnitude. Assume quasistatic fields and choose the loop normal so the wire's field through the loop is positive.
permittedResults: $B(r)=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$ for a long straight wire.
problems.strategy: First: Slice the loop into strips of area $a\,dr$ parallel to the wire. Next: Integrate from $r=x$ to $r=x+a$. Finally: Differentiate only the time-dependent current and use Lenz's law for direction.
hints: Slice the loop into strips of area $a\,dr$ parallel to the wire.
Integrate from $r=x$ to $r=x+a$.
Differentiate only the time-dependent current and use Lenz's law for direction.
problems.solution:
The flux is
$\Phi_B=\int_x^{x+a}\frac{\mu_0I(t)}{2\pi r}a\,dr
=\frac{\mu_0aI(t)}{2\pi}\ln\!\frac{x+a}{x}$.
Thus $|\mathcal E|=\frac{\mu_0a}{2\pi}\ln((x+a)/x)|dI/dt|$. The induced current produces flux opposite the increase. The logarithm is dimensionless and the prefactor times $dI/dt$ has units of volts.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Slice the loop into strips of area $a\,dr$ parallel to the wire.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Integrate from $r=x$ to $r=x+a$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Differentiate only the time-dependent current and use Lenz's law for direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wire field at the loop center times the area as an exact flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial field variation is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates the fixed geometry as though $x$ and $a$ varied in time.
commonErrors.consequence: Spurious emf terms are introduced.

problems.flawedProof: The field is uniform over the loop at $r=x$, so $\Phi_B=\mu_0Ia^2/(2\pi x)$ exactly. The fixed current geometry also contributes a derivative of $x$.

problems.title: Current continuity across an RL switch
problems.objective: Build a source-on and source-off RL solution with a continuous inductor current.
problems.statement: A $12\,\mathrm V$ source, $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor, and $2.0\,\mathrm H$ inductor are in series for a long time. At $t=0$ an ideal switch disconnects the source but leaves the resistor and inductor in a closed loop. Find $I(0^-)$, $I(0^+)$, and $I(t)$ for $t>0$. Find the initial inductor voltage under the passive sign convention used during the decay loop.
permittedResults: Kirchhoff's loop rule and continuity of finite-energy inductor current.
problems.strategy: First: At long time before switching, the ideal inductor acts as a zero-voltage branch. Next: The inductor current cannot jump without an impulse of voltage. Finally: Solve $L\,dI/dt+RI=0$ and use $v_L=L\,dI/dt$.
hints: At long time before switching, the ideal inductor acts as a zero-voltage branch.
The inductor current cannot jump without an impulse of voltage.
Solve $L\,dI/dt+RI=0$ and use $v_L=L\,dI/dt$.
problems.solution: Before switching, $I(0^-)=V/R=3.0\,\mathrm A$. Current continuity gives $I(0^+)=3.0\,\mathrm A$. The source-free loop has $\tau=L/R=0.50\,\mathrm s$, hence $I(t)=3.0e^{-t/0.50}\,\mathrm A$. With current referenced into the inductor's passive positive terminal, $v_L=L\,dI/dt=-RI$, so $v_L(0^+)=-12\,\mathrm V$. The polarity reverses relative to the charging stage so the inductor can sustain the decaying current.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: At long time before switching, the ideal inductor acts as a zero-voltage branch.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The inductor current cannot jump without an impulse of voltage.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Solve $L\,dI/dt+RI=0$ and use $v_L=L\,dI/dt$.

commonErrors.description: Sets the post-switch current instantly to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The required current continuity and finite-energy model are violated.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the charging-stage inductor voltage polarity during discharge.
commonErrors.consequence: The loop equation no longer sums to zero.

problems.flawedProof: Disconnecting the source makes $I(0^+)=0$. The inductor voltage remains $+12\,\mathrm V$ because inductors always oppose turning off.

problems.title: Energy and sign in coupled inductors
problems.objective: Evaluate mutual magnetic energy and test the passive-coupling bound.
problems.statement: Two coupled inductors have $L_1=4.0\,\mathrm H$, $L_2=9.0\,\mathrm H$, and $M=3.0\,\mathrm H$. Currents $i_1=1.0\,\mathrm A$ and $i_2=2.0\,\mathrm A$ both enter dotted terminals. Find the stored energy. Repeat when $i_2$ is reversed. Verify that the stated mutual inductance is compatible with a passive pair.
problems.strategy: First: Currents entering both dotted terminals use the positive mutual-energy sign. Next: Reverse only the mutual term when one current reverses. Finally: Compare $M^2$ with $L_1L_2$.
hints: Currents entering both dotted terminals use the positive mutual-energy sign.
Reverse only the mutual term when one current reverses.
Compare $M^2$ with $L_1L_2$.
problems.solution:
For both currents entering dotted terminals,
$U=\tfrac12(4)(1)^2+\tfrac12(9)(2)^2+(3)(1)(2)=2+18+6=26\,\mathrm J$.
Reversing $i_2$ changes the mutual term's sign, giving $U=2+18-6=14\,\mathrm J$. Finally, $M^2=9\,\mathrm{H^2}\le L_1L_2=36\,\mathrm{H^2}$, so the inductance matrix is positive definite and passive.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Currents entering both dotted terminals use the positive mutual-energy sign.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Reverse only the mutual term when one current reverses.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare $M^2$ with $L_1L_2$.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the mutual-energy sign unchanged after reversing one current.
commonErrors.consequence: The dot convention is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Checks $M\le L_1+L_2$ instead of $M^2\le L_1L_2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual positive-energy condition is not tested.

problems.flawedProof: The mutual term is always positive, so both current directions store $26\,\mathrm J$. Passivity follows because $M<L_1+L_2$.

problems.title: A load reflected to the transformer primary
problems.objective: Derive the impedance seen through an ideal transformer and verify power transfer.
problems.statement: An ideal transformer has turns ratio $a=N_p/N_s=4$. An $8.0\,\Omega$ resistor is connected across the secondary, and the primary is driven at $120\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. Find the impedance seen at the primary, the primary current, and the secondary voltage and current.
permittedResults: Ideal transformer voltage and current ratios.
problems.strategy: First: Use $V_p/V_s=a$ and $I_s/I_p=a$. Next: Derive $Z_{\rm in}=V_p/I_p$ rather than memorizing the direction of the square. Finally: Compare primary and secondary real powers.
hints: Use $V_p/V_s=a$ and $I_s/I_p=a$.
Derive $Z_{\rm in}=V_p/I_p$ rather than memorizing the direction of the square.
Compare primary and secondary real powers.
problems.solution: The secondary voltage is $V_s=120/4=30\,\mathrm V$, so $I_s=30/8.0=3.75\,\mathrm A$. The primary current is $I_p=I_s/a=0.9375\,\mathrm A$. Therefore $Z_{\rm in}=120/0.9375=128\,\Omega=a^2(8.0\,\Omega)$. Both sides transfer $112.5\,\mathrm W$, confirming the ratio orientation.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $V_p/V_s=a$ and $I_s/I_p=a$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Derive $Z_{\rm in}=V_p/I_p$ rather than memorizing the direction of the square.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare primary and secondary real powers.

commonErrors.description: Reflects the load as $Z_L/a^2=0.50\,\Omega$.
commonErrors.consequence: The turns-ratio direction is reversed and the primary current is grossly overstated.

commonErrors.description: Uses equal currents on both sides of an ideal transformer.
commonErrors.consequence: Power conservation fails.

problems.flawedProof: The primary sees $8/4^2=0.50\,\Omega$, so it draws $240\,\mathrm A$. Ideal coupling means the secondary current is also $240\,\mathrm A$.

problems.title: Energy exchange in an ideal LC circuit
problems.objective: Solve an LC initial-value problem and identify maximum current from energy conservation.
problems.statement: An ideal circuit has $C=10\,\mu\mathrm F$ initially charged to $V_0=100\,\mathrm V$ and $L=0.10\,\mathrm H$ with zero current. At $t=0$ the capacitor is connected to the inductor. Find $q(t)$, $I(t)$ under the convention $I=-dq/dt$, the total energy, and the maximum current.
problems.strategy: First: Use $q(0)=CV_0$ and $q'(0)=0$. Next: The angular frequency is $1/\sqrt{LC}$. Finally: At maximum current the capacitor charge is zero, so all energy is magnetic.
hints: The angular frequency is $1/\sqrt{LC}$.
At maximum current the capacitor charge is zero, so all energy is magnetic.
problems.solution: With $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=10^3\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, the charge is $q(t)=CV_0\cos(\omega_0t)$ and $I(t)=CV_0\omega_0\sin(\omega_0t)$. The conserved energy is $U=CV_0^2/2=0.050\,\mathrm J$. Hence $I_{\max}=V_0\sqrt{C/L}=1.0\,\mathrm A$, agreeing with the sinusoidal coefficient.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $q(0)=CV_0$ and $q'(0)=0$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The angular frequency is $1/\sqrt{LC}$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: At maximum current the capacitor charge is zero, so all energy is magnetic.

commonErrors.description: Uses exponential decay for an ideal lossless LC circuit.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy is made to disappear despite zero resistance.

commonErrors.description: Sets $I=q/C$.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge divided by capacitance is voltage, not current.

problems.flawedProof: The charge decays as $CV_0e^{-t/LC}$, and the current is $q/C$, so the maximum current is $100\,\mathrm A$.

problems.title: RL rise time and stored-energy checkpoint
problems.objective: Solve a source-driven RL transient and connect a current fraction to stored energy.
problems.statement: A series circuit with $V=18\,\mathrm V$, $R=6.0\,\Omega$, and $L=1.2\,\mathrm H$ is switched on from zero current. Find the time to reach $90\%$ of the final current and the magnetic energy stored at that instant.
problems.strategy: First: The final current is $V/R$ and the time constant is $L/R$. Next: Set $1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.90$ and solve with a logarithm. Finally: Use the actual $90\%$ current, not the final current, in the energy formula.
hints: The final current is $V/R$ and the time constant is $L/R$.
Set $1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.90$ and solve with a logarithm.
Use the actual $90\%$ current, not the final current, in the energy formula.
problems.solution: The final current is $3.0\,\mathrm A$ and $\tau=L/R=0.20\,\mathrm s$. Solving $e^{-t/\tau}=0.10$ gives $t=\tau\ln10=0.461\,\mathrm s$. The current is then $2.70\,\mathrm A$, so $U_L=\tfrac12(1.2)(2.70)^2=4.37\,\mathrm J$. Energy has reached $0.90^2=81\%$ of its final value because it is quadratic in current.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The final current is $V/R$ and the time constant is $L/R$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Set $1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.90$ and solve with a logarithm.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the actual $90\%$ current, not the final current, in the energy formula.

commonErrors.description: Uses $t=0.90\tau$.
commonErrors.consequence: An exponential fraction is treated as a linear ramp.

commonErrors.description: Says 90 percent current means 90 percent stored energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The quadratic current dependence is missed.

problems.flawedProof: The circuit reaches $90\%$ after $0.9\tau=0.18\,\mathrm s$, and it then stores $90\%$ of its final magnetic energy.

problems.title: Classify an RLC discharge
problems.objective: Use the characteristic roots to classify underdamped, critical, and overdamped response.
problems.statement: A source-free series RLC circuit has $L=1.0\,\mathrm H$ and $C=0.25\,\mathrm F$. Determine the critical resistance. Classify the response for $R=3.0\,\Omega$ and $R=5.0\,\Omega$, and state whether either classification depends on the initial capacitor charge.
problems.strategy: First: Compare $(R/L)^2$ with $4/(LC)$ or use $R_c=2\sqrt{L/C}$. Next: A resistance below critical gives complex-conjugate roots. Finally: Initial conditions set amplitudes, not the root classification.
hints: Compare $(R/L)^2$ with $4/(LC)$ or use $R_c=2\sqrt{L/C}$.
A resistance below critical gives complex-conjugate roots.
Initial conditions set amplitudes, not the root classification.
problems.solution: Critical damping occurs at $R_c=2\sqrt{L/C}=2\sqrt{1/0.25}=4.0\,\Omega$. Thus $R=3.0\,\Omega$ is underdamped and oscillatory, while $R=5.0\,\Omega$ is overdamped with two real decay rates. The initial charge and current determine the coefficients of the modes but do not alter the circuit's damping classification.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Compare $(R/L)^2$ with $4/(LC)$ or use $R_c=2\sqrt{L/C}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: A resistance below critical gives complex-conjugate roots.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Initial conditions set amplitudes, not the root classification.

commonErrors.description: Uses $R_c=\sqrt{L/C}$ without the factor two.
commonErrors.consequence: Both test cases can be misclassified.

commonErrors.description: Claims a sufficiently large initial charge makes an overdamped circuit oscillate.
commonErrors.consequence: Initial amplitude is confused with characteristic roots.

problems.flawedProof: The critical resistance is $\sqrt{L/C}=2\,\Omega$, so both circuits are overdamped. A large initial charge could still make either one oscillate.

problems.title: Current phase in a capacitive series RLC circuit
problems.objective: Compute impedance magnitude and the signed current-voltage phase relation.
problems.statement: A series RLC circuit has $R=10\,\Omega$, $L=0.10\,\mathrm H$, $C=100\,\mu\mathrm F$, and is driven at $\omega=100\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ with voltage amplitude $100\,\mathrm V$. Find the current amplitude and state whether current leads or lags the source voltage, including the phase magnitude.
problems.strategy: First: Compute $X_L$ and $X_C$ separately with SI capacitance. Next: Use $|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$. Finally: A negative net reactance means current leads the applied voltage.
hints: Compute $X_L$ and $X_C$ separately with SI capacitance.
Use $|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$.
A negative net reactance means current leads the applied voltage.
problems.solution: The reactances are $X_L=10\,\Omega$ and $X_C=100\,\Omega$, so $Z=10-i90\,\Omega$ and $|Z|=\sqrt{8200}=90.6\,\Omega$. The current amplitude is $I_0=100/90.6=1.10\,\mathrm A$. The impedance angle is $\phi_Z=\tan^{-1}(-90/10)=-83.7^\circ$, so the current leads the source voltage by $83.7^\circ$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Compute $X_L$ and $X_C$ separately with SI capacitance.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: A negative net reactance means current leads the applied voltage.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two reactance magnitudes instead of subtracting their signed contributions.
commonErrors.consequence: The impedance and phase are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Says current lags because an inductor is present.
commonErrors.consequence: The much larger capacitive reactance is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The reactance is $X_L+X_C=110\,\Omega$, and any circuit containing an inductor makes current lag, so the current lags by nearly $90^\circ$.

problems.title: Emf between the ends of a rotating rod
problems.objective: Integrate motional emf when speed varies along a conductor.
problems.statement: A conducting rod of length $0.30\,\mathrm m$ rotates in its plane about one end at $20\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. A uniform $0.80\,\mathrm T$ magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane. Find the magnitude of the potential difference between the pivot and free end, and state why $B\ell v_{\rm end}$ is not exact here.
problems.strategy: First: A point at radius $r$ moves at speed $\omega r$. Next: Integrate $B\omega r\,dr$ from the pivot to the free end. Finally: Compare the average speed along the rod with the end speed.
hints: A point at radius $r$ moves at speed $\omega r$.
Integrate $B\omega r\,dr$ from the pivot to the free end.
Compare the average speed along the rod with the end speed.
problems.solution: The motional potential magnitude is $\mathcal E=\int_0^\ell B\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega\ell^2$. Numerically this is $\tfrac12(0.80)(20)(0.30)^2=0.72\,\mathrm V$. The shortcut $B\ell v_{\rm end}$ would give twice this value because the speed grows linearly from zero to $v_{\rm end}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: A point at radius $r$ moves at speed $\omega r$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Integrate $B\omega r\,dr$ from the pivot to the free end.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compare the average speed along the rod with the end speed.

commonErrors.description: Uses the free-end speed for every point of the rod.
commonErrors.consequence: The emf is overestimated by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Uses angular speed as though it were a linear speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression has incorrect dimensions.

problems.flawedProof: Every part of the rod moves at $v=\omega\ell$, so $\mathcal E=B\ell(\omega\ell)=1.44\,\mathrm V$.

problems.title: Center-to-rim voltage of a Faraday disk
problems.objective: Compute radial charge separation in a rotating conducting disk.
problems.statement: A conducting disk of radius $0.20\,\mathrm m$ rotates at $30\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ about its axis in a uniform axial field $0.40\,\mathrm T$. Find the magnitude of the center-to-rim potential difference. For positive $\omega$ and $\mathbf B$ both along $+z$, identify the higher-potential location.
permittedResults: $\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ and $\mathcal E=\int(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$.
problems.strategy: First: At radius $r$, the material velocity is $\omega r\mathbf e_\phi$. Next: For $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf B$ along $+z$, evaluate $\mathbf e_\phi\times\mathbf e_z$. Finally: Integrate the radial force per charge from $0$ to $R$.
hints: At radius $r$, the material velocity is $\omega r\mathbf e_\phi$.
For $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf B$ along $+z$, evaluate $\mathbf e_\phi\times\mathbf e_z$.
Integrate the radial force per charge from $0$ to $R$.
problems.solution: Here $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=\omega rB\mathbf e_r$, so positive charge is driven toward the rim. The rim is at higher potential, with $V_R-V_0=\int_0^R B\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega R^2=\tfrac12(0.40)(30)(0.20)^2=0.24\,\mathrm V$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: At radius $r$, the material velocity is $\omega r\mathbf e_\phi$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf B$ along $+z$, evaluate $\mathbf e_\phi\times\mathbf e_z$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Integrate the radial force per charge from $0$ to $R$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the circumference as the integration path even though charge separates radially.
commonErrors.consequence: The wrong geometry is used for the emf.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the cross product and declares the center positive.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted polarity is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: The emf is around the rim, so $\mathcal E=B(2\pi R)(\omega R)$. The magnetic force points inward, making the center positive.

problems.title: Flux changes through both field and area
problems.objective: Apply the product rule to a loop with simultaneous transformer and motional emf.
problems.statement: A rectangular conducting loop has fixed height $\ell$, time-dependent width $x(t)$, and lies perpendicular to a spatially uniform field $B(t)\mathbf e_z$. Choose the positive normal $+\mathbf e_z$. Derive the signed emf and identify the terms commonly called transformer and motional contributions.
problems.strategy: First: Write the flux as $\Phi_B=B(t)\ell x(t)$. Next: Differentiate both time-dependent factors. Finally: Check that either contribution disappears in its corresponding constant-field or fixed-area limit.
hints: Write the flux as $\Phi_B=B(t)\ell x(t)$.
Differentiate both time-dependent factors.
Check that either contribution disappears in its corresponding constant-field or fixed-area limit.
problems.solution:
The flux is $\Phi_B=B\ell x$, hence
$\mathcal E=-\ell\left(x\,\frac{dB}{dt}+B\,\frac{dx}{dt}\right)$.
The $-\ell x\,dB/dt$ term is associated with a nonconservative induced electric field in a changing magnetic field; the $-B\ell\,dx/dt$ term is the motional contribution from the moving boundary. Both have units of volts and their signs follow the common orientation convention.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Write the flux as $\Phi_B=B(t)\ell x(t)$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate both time-dependent factors.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check that either contribution disappears in its corresponding constant-field or fixed-area limit.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only the field and omits the changing area.
commonErrors.consequence: The motional emf vanishes incorrectly.

commonErrors.description: Adds a second overall minus sign to the motional term.
commonErrors.consequence: The two contributions are combined with an inconsistent orientation.

problems.flawedProof: Only explicit time variation of $B$ matters, so $\mathcal E=-\ell x\,dB/dt$. Motion of the boundary cannot affect flux.

problems.title: Terminal speed from eddy-current drag
problems.objective: Solve a simple magnetic-braking model and account for gravitational power.
problems.statement: A magnet of mass $m$ falls vertically through a conducting tube. Over the speed range of interest, model the upward eddy-current drag as $F_d=kv$, with $k>0$, and neglect buoyancy. Starting from rest, find $v(t)$ and the terminal speed. At terminal speed, identify the rate at which gravitational potential energy becomes heat.
permittedResults: Newton's second law and a first-order linear differential equation.
problems.strategy: First: Take downward as positive and write $m\,dv/dt=mg-kv$. Next: Use $v(0)=0$ to fix the exponential. Finally: At terminal speed, compare $mgv_t$ with $kv_t^2$.
hints: Take downward as positive and write $m\,dv/dt=mg-kv$.
Use $v(0)=0$ to fix the exponential.
At terminal speed, compare $mgv_t$ with $kv_t^2$.
problems.solution: The equation is $m\dot v+kv=mg$, so $v(t)=(mg/k)(1-e^{-kt/m})$. The terminal speed is $v_t=mg/k$. At terminal speed the gravitational power is $mgv_t=m^2g^2/k$, while drag dissipates $kv_t^2=m^2g^2/k$. The kinetic energy is then constant, so all continuing potential-energy loss becomes heat in the tube and magnet.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Take downward as positive and write $m\,dv/dt=mg-kv$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $v(0)=0$ to fix the exponential.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: At terminal speed, compare $mgv_t$ with $kv_t^2$.

commonErrors.description: Sets terminal speed to $k/(mg)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The force balance is inverted and dimensions are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims heating stops once acceleration becomes zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Zero net force is confused with zero opposing forces and zero power flow.

problems.flawedProof: Terminal speed occurs when $v_t=k/(mg)$. Since acceleration is then zero, neither gravity nor drag does work and no heat is produced.

problems.title: Sliding rod with circuit inductance
problems.objective: Solve an inductive motional-emf transient and prove its instantaneous power balance.
problems.statement: A rod of length $\ell$ is pulled at constant speed $v$ on rails in a uniform perpendicular field $B$. The closed circuit has resistance $R$, inductance $L$, and initial current zero. Derive $I(t)$, the magnetic drag, and an instantaneous identity relating external mechanical power, Joule heating, and magnetic-energy growth.
problems.strategy: First: The circuit equation is $L\dot I+RI=B\ell v$. Next: Solve the constant-forcing first-order equation with $I(0)=0$. Finally: Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and identify $LI\dot I=d(LI^2/2)/dt$.
hints: The circuit equation is $L\dot I+RI=B\ell v$.
Solve the constant-forcing first-order equation with $I(0)=0$.
Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and identify $LI\dot I=d(LI^2/2)/dt$.
problems.solution:
The current is $I(t)=(B\ell v/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L})$. Lenz's law makes the magnetic force oppose the motion, with magnitude $F=B\ell I$. Thus the external power needed for constant speed is $P_{\rm ext}=B\ell vI$. Multiplying $L\dot I+RI=B\ell v$ by $I$ gives
$P_{\rm ext}=I^2R+LI\dot I=I^2R+d(LI^2/2)/dt$.
Early work builds the field as well as heating the resistor; at long time all input power is Joule heat.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The circuit equation is $L\dot I+RI=B\ell v$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Solve the constant-forcing first-order equation with $I(0)=0$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and identify $LI\dot I=d(LI^2/2)/dt$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the final current immediately at switching.
commonErrors.consequence: Inductor-current continuity and magnetic-energy buildup are lost.

commonErrors.description: Equates external power to Joule heat at every instant.
commonErrors.consequence: The transient magnetic-energy term is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: The current instantly equals $B\ell v/R$, so $P_{\rm ext}=I^2R$ at every time and the inductor never changes the energy balance.

problems.title: Magnetic braking of a freely sliding rod
problems.objective: Couple motional emf to mechanical deceleration and recover all initial kinetic energy as heat.
problems.statement: A conducting rod of mass $m$ and length $\ell$ slides without mechanical friction on horizontal rails through a uniform perpendicular field $B$. The rail-rod circuit has resistance $R$ and negligible inductance. At $t=0$ the rod speed is $v_0$, and no external force acts afterward. Derive $v(t)$, the current, and the total Joule heat as $t\to\infty$.
problems.strategy: First: Use Lenz's law to put the magnetic force opposite $v$. Next: Solve $m\dot v=-(B^2\ell^2/R)v$. Finally: Integrate $I^2R$ or use the mechanical-energy equation as an independent check.
hints: Use Lenz's law to put the magnetic force opposite $v$.
Solve $m\dot v=-(B^2\ell^2/R)v$.
Integrate $I^2R$ or use the mechanical-energy equation as an independent check.
problems.solution:
The current magnitude is $I=B\ell v/R$, and magnetic drag gives $m\dot v=-(B^2\ell^2/R)v$. Hence
$v(t)=v_0e^{-t/\tau_m}$ with $\tau_m=mR/(B^2\ell^2)$, and $I(t)=(B\ell v_0/R)e^{-t/\tau_m}$.
The heat is
$Q=\int_0^\infty I^2R\,dt=(B^2\ell^2v_0^2/R)(\tau_m/2)=mv_0^2/2$.
It exactly equals the lost kinetic energy.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use Lenz's law to put the magnetic force opposite $v$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Solve $m\dot v=-(B^2\ell^2/R)v$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Integrate $I^2R$ or use the mechanical-energy equation as an independent check.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the magnetic force the same sign as velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted rod accelerates and energy grows without an external source.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the current rather than $I^2R$ to calculate heat.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge is confused with energy.

problems.flawedProof: The induced current pushes the rod forward, so $v=v_0e^{+t/\tau_m}$. Heat is $\int I\,dt$, which equals the initial momentum.

problems.title: An expanding loop that also rotates
problems.objective: Differentiate a flux containing changing area and changing orientation.
problems.statement: A circular loop in a uniform field $B$ has radius $r(t)=r_0(1+\alpha t)$ and its normal makes angle $\theta(t)=\omega t$ with the field. Choose the positive normal used in $\theta$. Derive the signed emf, and identify the separate area-change and rotation terms.
problems.strategy: First: Write $\Phi_B=B\pi r_0^2(1+\alpha t)^2\cos(\omega t)$. Next: Differentiate both the squared-radius factor and the cosine. Finally: Check the limits $\alpha=0$ and $\omega=0$.
hints: Write $\Phi_B=B\pi r_0^2(1+\alpha t)^2\cos(\omega t)$.
Differentiate both the squared-radius factor and the cosine.
Check the limits $\alpha=0$ and $\omega=0$.
problems.solution:
Differentiating the flux gives
$\mathcal E=-B\pi r_0^2\left[2\alpha(1+\alpha t)\cos(\omega t)-\omega(1+\alpha t)^2\sin(\omega t)\right]$.
The first term comes from changing area and the second from changing orientation. Setting $\alpha=0$ recovers the rotating-coil sine emf; setting $\omega=0$ leaves the emf opposing the growing area in a fixed field.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Write $\Phi_B=B\pi r_0^2(1+\alpha t)^2\cos(\omega t)$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate both the squared-radius factor and the cosine.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check the limits $\alpha=0$ and $\omega=0$.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only the cosine and treats the radius as constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The motional area-change contribution is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $(1+\alpha t)^2$ as $\alpha$.
commonErrors.consequence: The product and chain rules are applied incorrectly.

problems.flawedProof: Only rotation induces emf, so $\mathcal E=B\pi r_0^2\omega\sin(\omega t)$ even while the loop expands.

problems.title: Secondary transient driven by a primary current ramp
problems.objective: Solve an open- and closed-secondary mutual-induction response with explicit polarity.
problems.statement: Two coils have mutual inductance $M>0$ under a declared dot convention. The primary current is ramped as $i_1(t)=\alpha t$ for $t\ge0$, with $\alpha>0$. First find the open-circuit secondary emf. Then connect the secondary to a series resistance $R_2$ while retaining its self-inductance $L_2$ and initial current zero. Choose secondary current so the mutual source appears as $-M\alpha$ in its loop equation, and derive $i_2(t)$.
permittedResults: Coupled-inductor voltage laws and a first-order RL solution.
problems.strategy: First: The primary derivative is the constant $\alpha$. Next: For the chosen secondary reference, write $L_2\dot i_2+R_2i_2=-M\alpha$. Finally: Use $i_2(0)=0$ and check both the initial slope and long-time current.
hints: The primary derivative is the constant $\alpha$.
For the chosen secondary reference, write $L_2\dot i_2+R_2i_2=-M\alpha$.
Use $i_2(0)=0$ and check both the initial slope and long-time current.
problems.solution:
The open-circuit secondary voltage has magnitude $M\alpha$ and polarity opposing the increasing primary-linked flux. With the declared current reference, the closed-loop equation is $L_2\dot i_2+R_2i_2=-M\alpha$. Therefore
