$i_2(t)=-(M\alpha/R_2)(1-e^{-R_2t/L_2})$.
Initially $\dot i_2(0)=-M\alpha/L_2$, and at long time $i_2\to-M\alpha/R_2$, both consistent with the equation and Lenz's law.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The primary derivative is the constant $\alpha$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: For the chosen secondary reference, write $L_2\dot i_2+R_2i_2=-M\alpha$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use $i_2(0)=0$ and check both the initial slope and long-time current.

commonErrors.description: Uses $Mi_1=M\alpha t$ as the secondary emf.
commonErrors.consequence: Flux linkage is confused with its time derivative.

commonErrors.description: Chooses a secondary current that reinforces the increasing primary flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The mutual sign violates the declared dot convention and Lenz's law.

problems.flawedProof: The secondary source is $M\alpha t$, so $i_2=(M\alpha/R_2)t$ and grows without bound while reinforcing the primary field.

problems.title: An RL circuit driven by a finite voltage pulse
problems.objective: Construct a continuous piecewise transient across pulse turn-on and turn-off.
problems.statement: A series $RL$ circuit starts with zero current. A voltage $V_0$ is applied for $0<t<T$ and is then set to zero without opening the resistor-inductor loop. Derive $I(t)$ for all $t\ge0$ and verify current continuity at $t=T$.
permittedResults: $\tau=L/R$ and the standard constant-source RL solution.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the source-on interval from $I(0)=0$. Next: Use the resulting $I(T^-)$ as the initial value for source-free decay. Finally: Write the second exponential in elapsed time $t-T$.
hints: Solve the source-on interval from $I(0)=0$.
Use the resulting $I(T^-)$ as the initial value for source-free decay.
Write the second exponential in elapsed time $t-T$.
problems.solution:
Let $\tau=L/R$. During the pulse,
$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ for $0\le t\le T$.
Thus $I(T^-)=\frac{V_0}{R}(1-e^{-T/\tau})$. Current continuity gives the same value at $T^+$, and afterward
$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}(1-e^{-T/\tau})e^{-(t-T)/\tau}$ for $t\ge T$.
Both pieces agree at $T$ and the second decays to zero.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Solve the source-on interval from $I(0)=0$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use the resulting $I(T^-)$ as the initial value for source-free decay.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Write the second exponential in elapsed time $t-T$.

commonErrors.description: Restarts the post-pulse decay from $V_0/R$ regardless of pulse duration.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual current accumulated during the pulse is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Uses $e^{-t/\tau}$ instead of $e^{-(t-T)/\tau}$ after switch-off.
commonErrors.consequence: The decay is discontinuous at the switching time.

problems.flawedProof: At $t=T$ the current jumps to $V_0/R$ and then follows $(V_0/R)e^{-t/\tau}$, since each stage has its own independent initial condition.

problems.title: Normal modes of two magnetically coupled LC circuits
problems.objective: Diagonalize a symmetric coupled-inductor model and interpret its frequency splitting.
problems.statement: Two identical lossless circuits each contain capacitance $C$ and self-inductance $L$. Their inductors have mutual inductance $M$ with $0<M<L$. With currents defined into corresponding dotted terminals, the charge equations are $(Lq_1''+Mq_2'')+q_1/C=0$ and $(Mq_1''+Lq_2'')+q_2/C=0$. Find the in-phase and out-of-phase normal-mode frequencies.
problems.strategy: First: Try the symmetric mode $q_2=q_1$ and antisymmetric mode $q_2=-q_1$. Next: Each substitution replaces $L$ by an effective $L\pm M$. Finally: Check that both frequencies approach $1/\sqrt{LC}$ as $M\to0$.
hints: Try the symmetric mode $q_2=q_1$ and antisymmetric mode $q_2=-q_1$.
Each substitution replaces $L$ by an effective $L\pm M$.
Check that both frequencies approach $1/\sqrt{LC}$ as $M\to0$.
problems.solution: For $q_2=q_1$, the equation is $(L+M)q_1''+q_1/C=0$, so $\omega_+=1/\sqrt{C(L+M)}$. For $q_2=-q_1$, it is $(L-M)q_1''+q_1/C=0$, so $\omega_-=1/\sqrt{C(L-M)}$. Because $0<M<L$, both are real and the antisymmetric mode has the higher frequency. Both coalesce to $1/\sqrt{LC}$ when coupling vanishes.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Try the symmetric mode $q_2=q_1$ and antisymmetric mode $q_2=-q_1$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Each substitution replaces $L$ by an effective $L\pm M$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check that both frequencies approach $1/\sqrt{LC}$ as $M\to0$.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the same effective inductance to both modes.
commonErrors.consequence: The coupling produces no frequency splitting.

commonErrors.description: Claims the in-phase mode is faster despite its larger effective inductance.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse-square-root dependence is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: Both modes see $L+M$, so they have the same frequency. The in-phase mode is faster because adding inductance increases frequency.

problems.title: Inductance per length of a coaxial line
problems.objective: Derive coaxial inductance from magnetic field energy in the annular region.
problems.statement: A long ideal coaxial line has inner-conductor radius $a$ and outer-conductor inner radius $b>a$. Equal opposite currents $I$ flow on the conductors, fields in the metals and outside are neglected, and the annulus has permeability $\mu$. Derive the inductance per unit length using the magnetic field and energy density.
permittedResults: $B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)$ in the annulus and $u_B=B^2/(2\mu)$.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate energy over an annular shell of volume per length $2\pi r\,dr$. Next: Set the resulting energy per length equal to $L'I^2/2$. Finally: Check that the logarithm contains the dimensionless ratio $b/a$.
hints: Integrate energy over an annular shell of volume per length $2\pi r\,dr$.
Set the resulting energy per length equal to $L'I^2/2$.
Check that the logarithm contains the dimensionless ratio $b/a$.
problems.solution:
The energy per unit length is
$U'=\int_a^b\frac{B^2}{2\mu}2\pi r\,dr
=\int_a^b\frac{\mu I^2}{4\pi r}\,dr
=\frac{\mu I^2}{4\pi}\ln\frac ba$.
Since $U'=L'I^2/2$, the inductance per length is $L'=\frac{\mu}{2\pi}\ln(b/a)$. It is positive for $b>a$ and has units $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Integrate energy over an annular shell of volume per length $2\pi r\,dr$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Set the resulting energy per length equal to $L'I^2/2$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the logarithm contains the dimensionless ratio $b/a$.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the field rather than magnetic energy density over volume.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting quantity is not energy and cannot determine inductance.

commonErrors.description: Writes $\ln(b-a)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The logarithm has a dimensional argument and the radial integral is wrong.

problems.flawedProof: The inductance is proportional to $\int_a^b B\,dr$, giving $L'=\mu\ln(b-a)/(2\pi)$.

problems.title: Force from position-dependent inductance
problems.objective: Use magnetic coenergy to find actuator force and state the electrical constraint.
problems.statement: An ideal magnetic actuator has inductance $L(x)$ that increases as a movable iron plunger advances in $+x$. A current-regulated source holds current $I$ fixed quasistatically. Derive the magnetic force on the plunger. Explain why differentiating $LI^2/2$ at fixed flux linkage would give a different intermediate sign and why the source must be included in the energy accounting.
permittedResults: For a linear magnetic system at fixed current, $F_x=\partial(LI^2/2)/\partial x$.
problems.strategy: First: The current source performs electrical work while $L(x)$ changes. Next: Differentiate magnetic coenergy at fixed $I$. Finally: Use $dL/dx>0$ to interpret the force direction.
hints: The current source performs electrical work while $L(x)$ changes.
Differentiate magnetic coenergy at fixed $I$.
Use $dL/dx>0$ to interpret the force direction.
problems.solution:
For a linear system the magnetic coenergy is $W'=L(x)I^2/2$. At fixed current,
$F_x=(\partial W'/\partial x)_I=\tfrac12I^2\,dL/dx$.
Since $dL/dx>0$, the force pulls the plunger toward greater inductance. If flux linkage rather than current were fixed, the appropriate energy derivative uses a different controlled variable. At fixed current the source supplies the extra electrical work, so differentiating field energy alone while pretending the source does no work produces the misleading sign.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The current source performs electrical work while $L(x)$ changes.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate magnetic coenergy at fixed $I$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use $dL/dx>0$ to interpret the force direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses $F=-I^2(dL/dx)/2$ while also claiming current is fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: A fixed-flux energy derivative is mixed with a fixed-current constraint.

commonErrors.description: Omits the current source from the energy balance.
commonErrors.consequence: The change of magnetic energy is incorrectly equated to mechanical work alone.

problems.flawedProof: Because systems minimize magnetic energy, $F_x=-\tfrac12I^2dL/dx$, even though the ideal source keeps $I$ fixed and does no work.

problems.title: Lenz law and energy flow in an inductive sliding-rod circuit
problems.objective: Reconcile signed flux, an RL transient, magnetic drag, and mechanical-to-electrical energy flow.
problems.statement: Two horizontal conducting rails are separated by distance $\ell$ and joined at their left ends. A conducting rod bridges the rails on the right and is pulled rightward at prescribed constant speed $v_0>0$, so the loop area increases. A uniform external field $\mathbf B=-B\mathbf e_z$, $B>0$, points into the page. The complete loop has resistance $R>0$ and self-inductance $L>0$, both constant. At $t=0$ the constant-speed stage begins with $I(0)=0$. Take counterclockwise current as positive. Derive the signed circuit equation and current, the magnetic and required pulling forces, and an instantaneous energy balance. Check early- and late-time limits and explain why the magnetic force on each mobile charge does no work even though mechanical energy becomes heat and field energy.
permittedResults: $\mathcal E=-d\Phi_{\rm ext}/dt$, $L\dot I+RI=\mathcal E$, and $\mathbf F=I\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf B$.
problems.strategy: First: Use the counterclockwise normal $+\mathbf e_z$ to assign the negative external flux before differentiating. Next: Solve the constant-emf RL equation from $I(0)=0$, then use the rod's current direction in $I\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf B$. Finally: Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and compare it with the pulling power $F_{\rm pull}v_0$.
hints: Use the counterclockwise normal $+\mathbf e_z$ to assign the negative external flux before differentiating.
Solve the constant-emf RL equation from $I(0)=0$, then use the rod's current direction in $I\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf B$.
Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and compare it with the pulling power $F_{\rm pull}v_0$.
problems.solution:
Counterclockwise circulation corresponds to $+\mathbf e_z$, while $\Phi_{\rm ext}=-B\ell x$. Hence $\mathcal E=-d\Phi_{\rm ext}/dt=B\ell v_0>0$, so the induced current is counterclockwise. The circuit equation is $L\dot I+RI=B\ell v_0$, giving
$I(t)=\frac{B\ell v_0}{R}(1-e^{-Rt/L})$.
On the right rod, counterclockwise current is upward; $I\ell\mathbf e_y\times(-B\mathbf e_z)=-IB\ell\mathbf e_x$, a leftward drag. Maintaining speed requires $\mathbf F_{\rm pull}=+IB\ell\mathbf e_x$. Thus
$P_{\rm pull}=IB\ell v_0=I(L\dot I+RI)=\frac{d}{dt}(LI^2/2)+I^2R$.
Initially $I=0$, so drag and power vanish while $\dot I=B\ell v_0/L$. At late time $I\to B\ell v_0/R$, field energy is constant, and all pulling power becomes heat. Microscopically, $q\mathbf v_{\rm charge}\times\mathbf B$ is perpendicular to each charge velocity; mechanical work enters through the external constraint and induced electric field, not direct magnetic work on a charge.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use the counterclockwise normal $+\mathbf e_z$ to assign the negative external flux before differentiating.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Solve the constant-emf RL equation from $I(0)=0$, then use the rod's current direction in $I\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf B$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Multiply the circuit equation by $I$ and compare it with the pulling power $F_{\rm pull}v_0$.

commonErrors.description: Chooses a clockwise current that makes the magnetic force assist the rod's motion.
commonErrors.consequence: Lenz's law and the mechanical-energy balance are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Sets pulling power equal to Joule heat during the entire transient.
commonErrors.consequence: The growing inductor-energy term is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: The increasing inward flux induces clockwise current, so the magnetic force pulls the rod right. Since magnetic forces do work, $P_{\rm pull}=I^2R$ immediately and the inductance stores no energy.

problems.title: Emf of a moving wire with a nonuniform velocity
problems.objective: Evaluate the Lorentz-force line integral along a deforming conductor.
problems.statement: At one instant a straight conducting wire occupies $0\le y\le\ell$ along the $y$-axis in a uniform field $\mathbf B=B\mathbf e_z$. Its local material velocity is $\mathbf u(y)=u_0(y/\ell)\mathbf e_x$. There is no applied electric field. Find the open-circuit emf from $y=0$ to $y=\ell$, and compare it with the result obtained by assigning every point the endpoint speed $u_0$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute $\mathbf e_x\times\mathbf e_z=-\mathbf e_y$. Next: Integrate the linearly varying speed along $d\boldsymbol\ell=dy\mathbf e_y$. Finally: The average material speed is $u_0/2$.
hints: Compute $\mathbf e_x\times\mathbf e_z=-\mathbf e_y$.
Integrate the linearly varying speed along $d\boldsymbol\ell=dy\mathbf e_y$.
The average material speed is $u_0/2$.
problems.solution:
The magnetic force per positive charge is $\mathbf u\times\mathbf B=-Bu_0(y/\ell)\mathbf e_y$. Therefore
$\mathcal E_{0\to\ell}=\int_0^\ell-Bu_0\frac y\ell\,dy=-\frac12Bu_0\ell$.
The endpoint-speed shortcut would give $-Bu_0\ell$, twice the correct magnitude. The sign says the lower endpoint is at higher electrostatic potential after charge separation under the chosen integration direction.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Compute $\mathbf e_x\times\mathbf e_z=-\mathbf e_y$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Integrate the linearly varying speed along $d\boldsymbol\ell=dy\mathbf e_y$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The average material speed is $u_0/2$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the endpoint speed uniformly along the wire.
commonErrors.consequence: The emf is doubled.

commonErrors.description: Reverses $\mathbf u\times\mathbf B$ to $\mathbf B\times\mathbf u$.
commonErrors.consequence: The polarity is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: Every point shares the endpoint speed, so $\mathcal E=Bu_0\ell$. The sign is positive because $\mathbf B\times\mathbf u$ points upward.

problems.title: A resistive ring under a magnetic-field ramp
problems.objective: Solve a self-inductive ring response and interpret the perfect-conductor limit.
problems.statement: A conducting ring has resistance $R$, self-inductance $L$, and effective area $A$. A uniform external field normal to the ring increases as $B_{\rm ext}(t)=\beta t$ for $t\ge0$, with $I(0)=0$. Choose positive current to create positive flux. Derive $I(t)$ and the total linked flux $\Phi_{\rm tot}=AB_{\rm ext}+LI$. Examine the limits $t\to\infty$ at fixed $R>0$ and $R\to0^+$ at fixed finite time.
problems.strategy: First: The constant forcing is $-A\beta$. Next: Solve the first-order equation with $I(0)=0$. Finally: Substitute the solution into $AB_{\rm ext}+LI$ before taking limits.
hints: The constant forcing is $-A\beta$.
Solve the first-order equation with $I(0)=0$.
Substitute the solution into $AB_{\rm ext}+LI$ before taking limits.
problems.solution:
The equation is $L\dot I+RI=-A\beta$, so
$I(t)=-(A\beta/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L})$.
Thus $\Phi_{\rm tot}=A\beta t-(LA\beta/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L})$. At long time with fixed $R>0$, the current approaches a constant while external flux keeps growing, so resistance prevents flux freezing. At fixed finite $t$, as $R\to0^+$, $(1-e^{-Rt/L})/R\to t/L$, giving $I\to-A\beta t/L$ and $\Phi_{\rm tot}\to0$, the ideal perfect-conductor flux-conservation limit.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The constant forcing is $-A\beta$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Solve the first-order equation with $I(0)=0$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Substitute the solution into $AB_{\rm ext}+LI$ before taking limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive induced current for a positive external-flux ramp.
commonErrors.consequence: The ring reinforces rather than opposes the flux change.

commonErrors.description: Takes $R=0$ by substituting directly into a formula containing $1/R$.
commonErrors.consequence: A removable limiting form is mistaken for a divergence.

problems.flawedProof: The current is $+(A\beta/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L})$. As $R\to0$ it diverges, proving the perfect-conductor model is inconsistent.

problems.title: Critical RLC discharge from a charged capacitor
problems.objective: Derive the critically damped waveform, peak current, and complete energy dissipation.
problems.statement: A source-free series RLC circuit begins with capacitor voltage $V_0>0$ and zero current. Let $q$ be charge on the initially positive capacitor plate and define discharge current $I=-dq/dt$. Set $R=2\sqrt{L/C}$. Derive $q(t)$ and $I(t)$, find the time and value of maximum current, and show that all initial energy is ultimately dissipated in the resistor.
problems.strategy: First: At critical damping, write $q=(A+Bt)e^{-t/\sqrt{LC}}$ and impose both initial conditions. Next: Differentiate carefully using $I=-q'$. Finally: Use the circuit equation to show $dU/dt=-I^2R$ and evaluate endpoint energies.
hints: At critical damping, write $q=(A+Bt)e^{-t/\sqrt{LC}}$ and impose both initial conditions.
Differentiate carefully using $I=-q'$.
Use the circuit equation to show $dU/dt=-I^2R$ and evaluate endpoint energies.
problems.solution:
Let $\alpha=1/\sqrt{LC}$. Critical damping gives $q=(A+Bt)e^{-\alpha t}$. From $q(0)=CV_0$ and $q'(0)=0$, $A=CV_0$ and $B=\alpha CV_0$. Hence
$q(t)=CV_0(1+\alpha t)e^{-\alpha t}$,
$I(t)=-q'(t)=(V_0/L)t e^{-\alpha t}$.
The factor $te^{-\alpha t}$ peaks at $t=1/\alpha=\sqrt{LC}$, so $I_{\max}=V_0\sqrt{C/L}/e$. Multiplying the circuit equation by $I=-q'$ gives $d[q^2/(2C)+LI^2/2]/dt=-I^2R$. Both $q$ and $I$ tend to zero, so integrating shows $\int_0^\infty I^2R\,dt=CV_0^2/2$, the entire initial energy.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: At critical damping, write $q=(A+Bt)e^{-t/\sqrt{LC}}$ and impose both initial conditions.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate carefully using $I=-q'$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the circuit equation to show $dU/dt=-I^2R$ and evaluate endpoint energies.

commonErrors.description: Drops the linear-in-time factor from the repeated-root solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero-current initial condition cannot be satisfied.

commonErrors.description: Locates peak current at $t=0$ because capacitor voltage is initially largest.
commonErrors.consequence: Inductor-current continuity is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Critical damping gives $q=CV_0e^{-\alpha t}$, so $I(0)=CV_0\alpha$ is the maximum. The remaining field energy is lost without passing through the resistor.

problems.title: Positive energy and the coupling coefficient
problems.objective: Derive the mutual-inductance bound from positivity for arbitrary currents.
problems.statement: A linear two-coil system has magnetic energy $U=\tfrac12L_1i_1^2+Mi_1i_2+\tfrac12L_2i_2^2$, where $L_1,L_2>0$. Prove that nonnegative energy for every real current pair requires $M^2\le L_1L_2$. Interpret equality and define the coupling coefficient $k=M/\sqrt{L_1L_2}$.
permittedResults: Completing the square or the determinant criterion for a symmetric quadratic form.
problems.strategy: First: Treat $U$ as a quadratic polynomial in one current while the other is fixed. Next: Complete the square and require the remaining coefficient to be nonnegative. Finally: Equality makes one nonzero current combination store zero energy in the idealized model.
hints: Treat $U$ as a quadratic polynomial in one current while the other is fixed.
Complete the square and require the remaining coefficient to be nonnegative.
Equality makes one nonzero current combination store zero energy in the idealized model.
problems.solution:
Completing the square in $i_1$ gives
$2U=L_1(i_1+Mi_2/L_1)^2+(L_2-M^2/L_1)i_2^2$.
For this to be nonnegative for every $i_1,i_2$, the second coefficient must satisfy $L_2-M^2/L_1\ge0$, hence $M^2\le L_1L_2$. Therefore $|k|\le1$. Equality makes the inductance matrix singular: the current pair $i_1=-Mi_2/L_1$ stores zero energy, representing ideal perfect coupling with a redundant flux mode. Real leakage generally gives $|k|<1$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Treat $U$ as a quadratic polynomial in one current while the other is fixed.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Complete the square and require the remaining coefficient to be nonnegative.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Equality makes one nonzero current combination store zero energy in the idealized model.

commonErrors.description: Argues only that $M\le L_1+L_2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed condition is neither necessary nor sufficient for all-current energy positivity.

commonErrors.description: Checks positivity only when the two currents have the same sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The current combination that can make the mutual term negative is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Since each self-inductance is positive, the energy is automatically positive. It is enough that $M<L_1+L_2$, and negative currents need not be checked.

problems.title: When the magnetic-flux rule combines transformer and motional emf
problems.objective: Derive the flux rule for a moving closed material loop and state its modeling boundary.
problems.statement:
Let $C(t)$ be a smooth closed material wire moving with local velocity $\mathbf u$, spanning an oriented surface $S(t)$. Assume smooth fields and nonrelativistic motion. Starting from $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and transport of magnetic flux through a moving surface, show that
$\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-d\Phi_B/dt$.
Explain which term is transformer emf, which is motional emf, and why this statement does not justify applying a single $B\ell v$ formula to arbitrary moving circuits.
permittedResults: Stokes' theorem and the transport identity for flux through a moving surface.
problems.strategy: First: Separate $d\Phi_B/dt$ into explicit field change and boundary-motion contributions. Next: Use Stokes' theorem on the explicit $\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ term. Finally: Match the moving-boundary contribution to $\oint(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ with a consistent orientation.
hints: Separate $d\Phi_B/dt$ into explicit field change and boundary-motion contributions.
Use Stokes' theorem on the explicit $\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ term.
Match the moving-boundary contribution to $\oint(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ with a consistent orientation.
problems.solution:
For a material surface moving with boundary velocity $\mathbf u$, the flux transport identity is
$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S(t)}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A
=\int_{S(t)}\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf A
-\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$,
with signs fixed by the common surface-boundary orientation. Maxwell-Faraday and Stokes give
$\oint_C\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\int_S\partial_t\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A$.
Combining the two equations yields
$\oint_C(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-d\Phi_B/dt$.
The $\mathbf E$ circulation is transformer emf and the $\mathbf u\times\mathbf B$ circulation is motional emf. The shortcut $B\ell v$ requires uniform mutually perpendicular geometry and a single contributing segment; arbitrary circuits require the full line integral and consistent material velocity.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Separate $d\Phi_B/dt$ into explicit field change and boundary-motion contributions.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use Stokes' theorem on the explicit $\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ term.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Match the moving-boundary contribution to $\oint(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ with a consistent orientation.

commonErrors.description: Adds transformer and motional contributions with independent orientation conventions.
commonErrors.consequence: Their signs need not reproduce the total flux derivative.

commonErrors.description: Applies $B\ell v$ globally even when field and velocity vary along the wire.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Lorentz-force line integral is replaced by an invalid shortcut.

problems.flawedProof: Faraday's law already says $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-d\Phi_B/dt$, so adding $\mathbf u\times\mathbf B$ double counts motion. Nevertheless every moving loop has emf $B\ell v$.

problems.title: Electric flux from an enclosed point charge
problems.objective: Apply Gauss's law to distinguish enclosed charge from surface shape.
problems.statement: A closed surface of arbitrary shape encloses a point charge of $+2.00\,\mathrm{nC}$ and no other charge. Find the net electric flux through the surface. Does the answer change if the charge is moved away from the center without crossing the surface?
problems.strategy: First: Only the net enclosed charge appears in the integral law. Next: Insert $Q_{\rm enc}=2.00\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C$. Finally: Separate the total flux from its nonuniform distribution over the surface.
hints: Only the net enclosed charge appears in the integral law.
Insert $Q_{\rm enc}=2.00\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C$.
Separate the total flux from its nonuniform distribution over the surface.
problems.solution: Gauss's law gives $\Phi_E=Q_{\rm enc}/\epsilon_0=(2.00\times10^{-9})/(8.854\times10^{-12})=2.26\times10^2\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$. Moving the charge inside changes the local field and therefore the distribution of flux density, but not the net flux. The answer changes only if charge crosses the surface or other enclosed charge changes.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Only the net enclosed charge appears in the integral law.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Insert $Q_{\rm enc}=2.00\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Separate the total flux from its nonuniform distribution over the surface.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the surface must be spherical before Gauss's law can be used for net flux.
commonErrors.consequence: A symmetry requirement for finding the field is incorrectly imposed on the flux law.

commonErrors.description: Sets the flux to zero when the charge is off center.
commonErrors.consequence: The answer is made dependent on location rather than enclosed charge.

problems.flawedProof: Because the surface is not specified to be spherical, Gauss's law cannot apply. If the charge is off center, positive and negative flux contributions cancel, giving zero.

problems.title: Displacement current between capacitor plates
problems.objective: Calculate Maxwell's displacement current from a changing electric field.
problems.statement: Between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor, a nearly uniform electric field increases at $3.00\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ over plate area $4.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Neglect fringing. Find the displacement current through the gap.
problems.strategy: First: For a uniform normal field, $\Phi_E=EA$. Next: The plate area is constant, so differentiate only the field. Finally: Check that the result has amperes as its unit.
hints: For a uniform normal field, $\Phi_E=EA$.
The plate area is constant, so differentiate only the field.
Check that the result has amperes as its unit.
problems.solution: The electric-flux rate is $d\Phi_E/dt=A\,dE/dt$. Thus $I_d=\epsilon_0 A\,dE/dt=(8.854\times10^{-12})(4.00\times10^{-4})(3.00\times10^{11})=1.06\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm A$. The displacement current is $1.06\,\mathrm{mA}$ in the direction associated with the increasing electric field.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: For a uniform normal field, $\Phi_E=EA$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The plate area is constant, so differentiate only the field.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the result has amperes as its unit.

commonErrors.description: Uses the field magnitude rather than its time derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculated quantity is not a current and has the wrong dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor $\epsilon_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Electric-flux rate is mistaken for displacement current.

problems.flawedProof: The displacement current is simply $A(dE/dt)=1.20\times10^8\,\mathrm A$ because changing field is current.

problems.title: Orienting the fields in a plane wave
problems.objective: Use the Poynting direction and vacuum amplitude relation to orient a wave.
problems.statement: A vacuum plane wave travels in the $+x$ direction. At one event its electric field points in the $+y$ direction with magnitude $150\,\mathrm{V/m}$. State the direction of the magnetic field and its magnitude at that event.
permittedResults: $\mathbf S=(1/\mu_0)\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and $E=cB$ in vacuum.
problems.strategy: First: Require $\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ to point along $+\hat{\mathbf x}$. Next: Use $\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}$. Finally: Compute $B=E/c$.
hints: Require $\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ to point along $+\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Use $\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Compute $B=E/c$.
problems.solution: The magnetic field points in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ because $\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}$. Its magnitude is $B=E/c=150/(2.998\times10^8)=5.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm T$. The three directions form the right-handed ordered triple $\mathbf E,\mathbf B,\mathbf k$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Require $\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ to point along $+\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Compute $B=E/c$.

commonErrors.description: Points the magnetic field in the negative z direction.
commonErrors.consequence: The Poynting vector then points opposite the stated propagation direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses $B=cE$.
commonErrors.consequence: The amplitude relation is inverted, producing wrong units and magnitude.

problems.flawedProof: The magnetic field is $cE=4.5\times10^{10}\,\mathrm T$ in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ so that it trails the electric field.

problems.title: Wavelength from frequency in vacuum
problems.objective: Relate the temporal and spatial scales of an electromagnetic wave.
problems.statement: A monochromatic electromagnetic wave in vacuum has frequency $2.40\,\mathrm{GHz}$. Find its period and wavelength.
problems.strategy: First: Convert gigahertz to $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Next: Take the reciprocal to find the period. Finally: Divide the vacuum wave speed by the frequency to find wavelength.
hints: Convert gigahertz to $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Take the reciprocal to find the period.
Divide the vacuum wave speed by the frequency to find wavelength.
problems.solution: With $f=2.40\times10^9\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $T=1/f=4.17\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm s=0.417\,\mathrm{ns}$. Also $\lambda=c/f=(2.998\times10^8)/(2.40\times10^9)=1.25\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm m$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Convert gigahertz to $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Take the reciprocal to find the period.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Divide the vacuum wave speed by the frequency to find wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Treats 2.40 GHz as 2.40 Hz.
commonErrors.consequence: Both period and wavelength are wrong by nine orders of magnitude.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies $c$ and $f$ to obtain wavelength.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression has incorrect dimensions.

problems.flawedProof: The wavelength is $cf=7.20\times10^{17}\,\mathrm m$ and the period is $2.40\,\mathrm{ns}$.

problems.title: Equal field energy densities in a vacuum wave
problems.objective: Compare the instantaneous electric and magnetic energy densities of a plane wave.
problems.statement: At the crest of a vacuum plane wave, the electric-field magnitude is $600\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Find the magnetic-field magnitude and the electric, magnetic, and total energy densities at that event.
problems.strategy: First: Find the magnetic field from the plane-wave amplitude relation. Next: Use $c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0)$ to compare the two energy terms. Finally: Add the two equal contributions for the total density.
hints: Find the magnetic field from the plane-wave amplitude relation.
Use $c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0)$ to compare the two energy terms.
Add the two equal contributions for the total density.
problems.solution: The magnetic field is $B=E/c=2.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T$. The electric density is $u_E=\epsilon_0E^2/2=1.59\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$. Substitution of $B=E/c$ and $c^{-2}=\mu_0\epsilon_0$ gives $u_B=u_E=1.59\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$. Therefore $u=3.19\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Find the magnetic field from the plane-wave amplitude relation.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0)$ to compare the two energy terms.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Add the two equal contributions for the total density.

commonErrors.description: Uses the peak field in an RMS energy formula with an extra factor of one half.
commonErrors.consequence: The instantaneous crest energy is undercounted.

commonErrors.description: Adds electric energy but omits magnetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The total wave energy density is too small by a factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: Only the electric field carries energy, so $u=\epsilon_0E^2/2=1.59\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$ and $B=0$.

problems.title: Average intensity from electric amplitude
problems.objective: Convert the peak electric field of a sinusoidal vacuum wave into average intensity.
problems.statement: A sinusoidal plane wave in vacuum has peak electric-field amplitude $E_0=300\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Find its time-averaged intensity.

hints: Identify the given field as a peak amplitude, not an RMS value.
Square the amplitude before multiplying by the vacuum constants.
Report the result in $\mathrm{W/m^2}$.
problems.solution: The average intensity is $\langle S\rangle=\tfrac12(2.998\times10^8)(8.854\times10^{-12})(300)^2=1.19\times10^2\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Identify the given field as a peak amplitude, not an RMS value.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Square the amplitude before multiplying by the vacuum constants.

commonErrors.description: Uses a field proportional rather than a field-squared relation.
