problems.title: Radiation pressure on absorbing and reflecting surfaces
problems.objective: Relate electromagnetic momentum flux to radiation pressure.
problems.statement: A normally incident beam has intensity $800\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$. Find the radiation pressure on (a) a perfectly absorbing surface and (b) a perfectly reflecting surface.
permittedResults: $p_{\rm abs}=I/c$ and $p_{\rm refl}=2I/c$ for normal incidence.
problems.strategy: First: An absorbed photon transfers its incoming momentum once. Next: Reflection reverses the normal momentum and doubles the transfer. Finally: Pressure is force per area and has pascal units.
hints: An absorbed photon transfers its incoming momentum once.
Reflection reverses the normal momentum and doubles the transfer.
Pressure is force per area and has pascal units.
problems.solution: For absorption, $p=I/c=800/(2.998\times10^8)=2.67\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. For perfect reflection, the normal momentum reverses, so $p=2I/c=5.34\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: An absorbed photon transfers its incoming momentum once.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Reflection reverses the normal momentum and doubles the transfer.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Pressure is force per area and has pascal units.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the factor of two to absorption rather than reflection.
commonErrors.consequence: The momentum change for each surface is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies intensity by c.
commonErrors.consequence: The result has the wrong units and is too large by a factor of c squared.

problems.flawedProof: The absorbing pressure is $2I/c$ because all light is captured, while reflection transfers no momentum because no energy is absorbed.

problems.title: Magnetic field inside and outside a charging capacitor
problems.objective: Use Ampere-Maxwell law on two radii in a parallel-plate capacitor gap.
problems.statement: A circular parallel-plate capacitor of plate radius $R=4.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ is charged by a steady current $I=0.300\,\mathrm A$. Neglect fringing and take the displacement current density as uniform. Find the magnetic-field magnitude in the gap at radii (a) $r=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ and (b) $r=6.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the axis.
problems.strategy: First: Inside the plate radius, the enclosed displacement current scales as $r^2/R^2$. Next: Outside the plates, the loop encloses the full displacement current. Finally: Use circular symmetry so that $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=B(2\pi r)$.
hints: Inside the plate radius, the enclosed displacement current scales as $r^2/R^2$.
Outside the plates, the loop encloses the full displacement current.
Use circular symmetry so that $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=B(2\pi r)$.
problems.solution: For $r<R$, $I_{d,\rm enc}=I r^2/R^2$, so $B=\mu_0Ir/(2\pi R^2)$. At $r=0.0200\,\mathrm m$, $B=7.50\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm T$. For $r>R$, the entire $0.300\,\mathrm A$ is enclosed, giving $B=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)=1.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T$ at $r=0.0600\,\mathrm m$. The field circulates by the right-hand rule around the displacement-current direction.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Inside the plate radius, the enclosed displacement current scales as $r^2/R^2$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Outside the plates, the loop encloses the full displacement current.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use circular symmetry so that $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=B(2\pi r)$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full charging current at every radius inside the plate area.
commonErrors.consequence: The interior field incorrectly varies as one over r and diverges on axis.

commonErrors.description: Sets the field to zero in the dielectric gap because no charges cross it.
commonErrors.consequence: The displacement-current term is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: No conduction current crosses the gap, so $B=0$ there. Outside the plates the magnetic field is also zero because the capacitor blocks current.

problems.title: Microwave scales in a dielectric
problems.objective: Compute wave speed, wavelength, and period in a nondispersive dielectric.
problems.statement: A $1.50\,\mathrm{GHz}$ electromagnetic wave travels in a lossless, nonmagnetic dielectric with relative permittivity $\epsilon_r=2.25$. Find its phase speed, wavelength, and period.
problems.strategy: First: For $\mu_r=1$, the refractive index is $n=\sqrt{\epsilon_r}$. Next: Frequency is unchanged by entering the medium. Finally: Use the medium speed, not c, when computing wavelength.
hints: For $\mu_r=1$, the refractive index is $n=\sqrt{\epsilon_r}$.
Frequency is unchanged by entering the medium.
Use the medium speed, not c, when computing wavelength.
problems.solution: Here $n=\sqrt{2.25}=1.50$, so $v=c/n=2.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=(2.00\times10^8)/(1.50\times10^9)=0.133\,\mathrm m$. The period depends only on frequency: $T=6.67\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm s$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: For $\mu_r=1$, the refractive index is $n=\sqrt{\epsilon_r}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Frequency is unchanged by entering the medium.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the medium speed, not c, when computing wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Uses c for the wavelength despite the dielectric.
commonErrors.consequence: The wavelength is too long by the refractive index.

commonErrors.description: Divides the frequency by the refractive index at the boundary.
commonErrors.consequence: Temporal continuity of the wave is violated.

problems.flawedProof: The dielectric lowers the frequency to $1.00\,\mathrm{GHz}$ but leaves the wavelength at $c/(1.50\,\mathrm{GHz})=0.200\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Instantaneous Poynting vector from crossed fields
problems.objective: Compute electromagnetic energy-flow direction and magnitude from field vectors.
problems.statement: At one point in vacuum, $\mathbf E=(200\,\mathrm{V/m})\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=(0.500\,\mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}$. Find the instantaneous Poynting vector.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Next: Convert microtesla to tesla before multiplying. Finally: This is an instantaneous value, so do not insert a sinusoidal averaging factor.
hints: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$.
Convert microtesla to tesla before multiplying.
This is an instantaneous value, so do not insert a sinusoidal averaging factor.
problems.solution: The cross product points in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Its magnitude is $S=EB/\mu_0=(200)(0.500\times10^{-6})/(4\pi\times10^{-7})=79.6\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$. Thus $\mathbf S=(79.6\,\mathrm{W/m^2})\hat{\mathbf z}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Convert microtesla to tesla before multiplying.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: This is an instantaneous value, so do not insert a sinusoidal averaging factor.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the cross product to B cross E.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy-flow direction is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Applies a factor one half to the specified instantaneous fields.
commonErrors.consequence: A time-average convention is used without sinusoidal amplitudes.

problems.flawedProof: Because magnetic field comes first physically, $\mathbf S=(\mathbf B\times\mathbf E)/\mu_0=-39.8\hat{\mathbf z}\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ after time averaging.

problems.title: Linear and circular polarization from phase
problems.objective: Classify polarization using component amplitudes and relative phase.
problems.statement: At a fixed point, compare two transverse electric fields: (a) $\mathbf E=E_0\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf x}+E_0\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf y}$; (b) $\mathbf E=E_0\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf x}+E_0\sin\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf y}$. Classify each polarization and describe the tip of $\mathbf E$.
permittedResults: The polarization curve is traced by the transverse electric-field tip at a fixed position.
problems.strategy: First: Eliminate time between the two component equations. Next: Equal in-phase components maintain a fixed component ratio. Finally: Equal quadrature components obey a constant-radius equation.
hints: Eliminate time between the two component equations.
Equal in-phase components maintain a fixed component ratio.
Equal quadrature components obey a constant-radius equation.
problems.solution: In (a), $E_y=E_x$ at all times, so the field oscillates along the fixed line $y=x$: linear polarization at $45^\circ$ to the x axis. In (b), $E_x^2+E_y^2=E_0^2$, so the tip traces a circle and the wave is circularly polarized. The handedness additionally depends on propagation direction and the sign convention for time.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Eliminate time between the two component equations.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Equal in-phase components maintain a fixed component ratio.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Equal quadrature components obey a constant-radius equation.

commonErrors.description: Calls both fields circular because their component amplitudes are equal.
commonErrors.consequence: The essential relative phase is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Assigns handedness without stating propagation direction.
commonErrors.consequence: A convention-dependent property is claimed from incomplete information.

problems.flawedProof: Equal x and y amplitudes always make a circle, so both waves are circularly polarized with the same handedness.

problems.title: Wave speed and impedance of a magnetic dielectric
problems.objective: Calculate propagation speed and intrinsic impedance from material parameters.
problems.statement: A lossless homogeneous medium has $\epsilon_r=4.00$ and $\mu_r=2.25$. Find the electromagnetic phase speed and intrinsic impedance.
problems.strategy: First: Write $v=c/\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}$. Next: Write $\eta=Z_0\sqrt{\mu_r/\epsilon_r}$. Finally: Keep speed and impedance ratios conceptually separate.
hints: Write $v=c/\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}$.
Write $\eta=Z_0\sqrt{\mu_r/\epsilon_r}$.
Keep speed and impedance ratios conceptually separate.
problems.solution: The refractive factor is $\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}=\sqrt9=3$, so $v=c/3=9.99\times10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The impedance is $\eta=Z_0\sqrt{2.25/4.00}=0.75Z_0=2.83\times10^2\,\Omega$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Write $v=c/\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Write $\eta=Z_0\sqrt{\mu_r/\epsilon_r}$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Keep speed and impedance ratios conceptually separate.

commonErrors.description: Uses the product of relative parameters in both speed and impedance.
commonErrors.consequence: The impedance fails to reflect the ratio of magnetic to electric response.

commonErrors.description: Reports c divided by epsilon-r rather than by the square-root product.
commonErrors.consequence: The material wave speed is calculated incorrectly.

problems.flawedProof: Both quantities depend on $\mu_r\epsilon_r=9$, so $v=c/9$ and $\eta=9Z_0$.

problems.title: Field amplitudes from measured intensity
problems.objective: Infer sinusoidal vacuum-wave field amplitudes from average power flux.
problems.statement: A detector measures average intensity $50.0\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ for a sinusoidal plane wave in vacuum. Find the peak electric- and magnetic-field amplitudes.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the time-averaged intensity expression for the peak electric amplitude. Next: Take the positive square root because amplitude is nonnegative. Finally: Use the vacuum field ratio for the magnetic amplitude.
hints: Solve the time-averaged intensity expression for the peak electric amplitude.
Take the positive square root because amplitude is nonnegative.
Use the vacuum field ratio for the magnetic amplitude.
problems.solution: The peak electric amplitude is $E_0=\sqrt{2I/(c\epsilon_0)}=\sqrt{100/[(2.998\times10^8)(8.854\times10^{-12})]}=1.94\times10^2\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Then $B_0=E_0/c=6.47\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm T$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Solve the time-averaged intensity expression for the peak electric amplitude.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Take the positive square root because amplitude is nonnegative.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use the vacuum field ratio for the magnetic amplitude.

commonErrors.description: Uses I rather than 2I under the square root for a peak amplitude.
commonErrors.consequence: An RMS field is reported as a peak field.

commonErrors.description: Takes intensity proportional to the field rather than its square.
commonErrors.consequence: Amplitude scaling and dimensions are wrong.

problems.flawedProof: Since $I=c\epsilon_0E_0$, the electric amplitude is $1.88\times10^4\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $B_0=cE_0$.

problems.title: Force from a laser on an absorbing panel
problems.objective: Convert incident intensity into radiation force on a finite absorber.
problems.statement: A normally incident beam of uniform intensity $1.00\,\mathrm{kW/m^2}$ falls on a perfectly absorbing panel of area $0.200\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Find the average force due to radiation pressure. Ignore edge effects.
problems.strategy: First: Convert kilowatts per square meter to SI base units. Next: Use the absorption, not reflection, pressure. Finally: Multiply pressure by the illuminated area.
hints: Convert kilowatts per square meter to SI base units.
Use the absorption, not reflection, pressure.
Multiply pressure by the illuminated area.
problems.solution: The pressure is $p=I/c=1000/(2.998\times10^8)=3.34\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. The force is $F=pA=(3.34\times10^{-6})(0.200)=6.67\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm N$, directed away from the source along the beam.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Convert kilowatts per square meter to SI base units.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use the absorption, not reflection, pressure.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Multiply pressure by the illuminated area.

commonErrors.description: Uses twice the momentum transfer for an absorbing panel.
commonErrors.consequence: The force is incorrectly doubled.

commonErrors.description: Treats intensity itself as a force.
commonErrors.consequence: Power per area is confused with momentum transfer per time.

problems.flawedProof: The panel receives $IA=200\,\mathrm N$ because every watt of absorbed light supplies one newton of force.

problems.title: Electric and magnetic phase in a traveling wave
problems.objective: Evaluate co-propagating plane-wave fields at a specified phase.
problems.statement: A vacuum plane wave traveling in $+x$ is $\mathbf E=E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$. Write $\mathbf B(x,t)$ and evaluate both fields at $x=\lambda/4$, $t=0$.
permittedResults: For a vacuum plane wave, $\mathbf B=(1/c)\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E$.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Next: Electric and magnetic fields in a vacuum traveling wave share the same phase. Finally: At $x=\lambda/4$, $kx=\pi/2$.
hints: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$.
Electric and magnetic fields in a vacuum traveling wave share the same phase.
At $x=\lambda/4$, $kx=\pi/2$.
problems.solution: The magnetic field is $\mathbf B=(E_0/c)\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}$. At $x=\lambda/4$ and $t=0$, the phase is $\pi/2$, so $\mathbf E=\mathbf0$ and $\mathbf B=\mathbf0$. Their simultaneous zeros reflect in-phase traveling-wave fields, not absent propagation everywhere.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Electric and magnetic fields in a vacuum traveling wave share the same phase.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: At $x=\lambda/4$, $kx=\pi/2$.

commonErrors.description: Shifts the magnetic field by a quarter cycle relative to the electric field.
commonErrors.consequence: A standing-wave phase relation is incorrectly assigned to a traveling wave.

commonErrors.description: Points B along negative z for propagation in positive x.
commonErrors.consequence: The Poynting vector points backward.

problems.flawedProof: Magnetic field must lag electric field by $90^\circ$, so at $x=\lambda/4$ the electric field is zero while $\mathbf B=(E_0/c)\hat{\mathbf z}$.

problems.title: Normal electric field at a dielectric interface
problems.objective: Apply Maxwell boundary conditions to a charge-free dielectric interface.
problems.statement: A static electric field is normal to an interface from medium 1 with $\epsilon_1=2\epsilon_0$ into medium 2 with $\epsilon_2=5\epsilon_0$. There is no free surface charge. If $E_{1n}=100\,\mathrm{V/m}$ points from 1 to 2, find $E_{2n}$.
problems.strategy: First: No free surface charge makes the normal component of D continuous. Next: Use $D_n=\epsilon E_n$ in each linear dielectric. Finally: Preserve the stated direction while changing the magnitude.
hints: No free surface charge makes the normal component of D continuous.
Use $D_n=\epsilon E_n$ in each linear dielectric.
Preserve the stated direction while changing the magnitude.
problems.solution: The boundary condition gives $D_{2n}=D_{1n}$, so $\epsilon_2E_{2n}=\epsilon_1E_{1n}$. Therefore $E_{2n}=(2/5)(100)=40.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$, still pointing from medium 1 to medium 2. Bound polarization charge accounts for the discontinuity in E even though free surface charge is zero.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: No free surface charge makes the normal component of D continuous.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $D_n=\epsilon E_n$ in each linear dielectric.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Preserve the stated direction while changing the magnitude.

commonErrors.description: Sets the normal electric fields equal because there is no free surface charge.
commonErrors.consequence: Continuity of D is confused with continuity of E.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the permittivity ratio.
commonErrors.consequence: The field incorrectly grows in the higher-permittivity material.

problems.flawedProof: Electric field is always continuous, so $E_{2n}=100\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Alternatively multiplying by $5/2$ gives $250\,\mathrm{V/m}$.

problems.title: Reflection phase at a perfect conductor
problems.objective: Determine reflected field signs from the conductor boundary condition.
problems.statement: A vacuum plane wave travels in $+x$ toward a perfect conductor at $x=0$. Its incident electric field at the surface is $E_0\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf y}$ and its incident magnetic field is $(E_0/c)\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf z}$. Give the reflected electric and magnetic fields at the surface and the total tangential electric field there.
permittedResults: The tangential electric field vanishes at a perfect conductor; each traveling vacuum wave satisfies the right-handed field relation.
problems.strategy: First: Cancel the incident tangential electric field at the surface. Next: The reflected wave travels in negative x, so recompute its B direction from k cross E. Finally: Add incident and reflected fields component by component.
hints: Cancel the incident tangential electric field at the surface.
The reflected wave travels in negative x, so recompute its B direction from k cross E.
Add incident and reflected fields component by component.
problems.solution: At the surface the reflected electric field must be $\mathbf E_r=-E_0\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf y}$, giving $\mathbf E_{\rm tot,t}=0$. For propagation in $-x$, $\mathbf B_r=(1/c)(-\hat{\mathbf x})\times\mathbf E_r=(E_0/c)\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf z}$. Thus the magnetic fields add at the surface while the electric fields cancel.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Cancel the incident tangential electric field at the surface.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The reflected wave travels in negative x, so recompute its B direction from k cross E.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Add incident and reflected fields component by component.

commonErrors.description: Reflects E without a sign reversal at the conducting surface.
commonErrors.consequence: The total tangential electric field violates the perfect-conductor boundary condition.

commonErrors.description: Reverses both E and B on reflection.
commonErrors.consequence: The reflected Poynting vector points in the wrong direction.

problems.flawedProof: Reflection reverses every vector, so $\mathbf E_r=-\mathbf E_i$ and $\mathbf B_r=-\mathbf B_i$. Both total fields therefore vanish at the metal.

problems.title: Energy and momentum in a finite light pulse
problems.objective: Compute the energy and absorbed momentum of a finite electromagnetic pulse.
problems.statement: A rectangular light pulse of intensity $400\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ illuminates area $3.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ for $2.00\,\mathrm{ms}$. The pulse is fully absorbed. Find its energy and the momentum delivered to the absorber.
problems.strategy: First: Intensity times area gives incident power. Next: Multiply power by the pulse duration after converting milliseconds. Finally: Absorption transfers the pulse momentum without the reflection factor of two.
hints: Intensity times area gives incident power.
Multiply power by the pulse duration after converting milliseconds.
Absorption transfers the pulse momentum without the reflection factor of two.
problems.solution: The pulse power is $IA=(400)(3.00\times10^{-2})=12.0\,\mathrm W$. Its energy is $U=(12.0)(2.00\times10^{-3})=2.40\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J$. Full absorption transfers $p=U/c=8.01\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ along the propagation direction.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Intensity times area gives incident power.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Multiply power by the pulse duration after converting milliseconds.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Absorption transfers the pulse momentum without the reflection factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Uses intensity directly as total power without multiplying by area.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy ignores the illuminated footprint.

commonErrors.description: Doubles the momentum for an absorbing target.
commonErrors.consequence: A reflection result is used for absorption.

problems.flawedProof: The energy is $I\Delta t=0.800\,\mathrm J$, and absorption reverses the light, so the momentum is $2U/c$.

problems.title: Momentum density and pressure from energy flow
problems.objective: Relate Poynting flux, electromagnetic momentum density, and absorbing pressure.
problems.statement: A steady collimated beam in vacuum has average Poynting magnitude $900\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$. Find its average electromagnetic momentum density and the pressure it exerts at normal incidence on a perfect absorber.
permittedResults: $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$ in vacuum and $p_{\rm abs}=S/c$.
problems.strategy: First: Momentum density is momentum per volume, not momentum flux. Next: Divide energy flux by c squared for density. Finally: Divide energy flux by c once for absorbed pressure.
hints: Momentum density is momentum per volume, not momentum flux.
Divide energy flux by c squared for density.
Divide energy flux by c once for absorbed pressure.
problems.solution: The momentum density is $g=S/c^2=900/(2.998\times10^8)^2=1.00\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. The absorbing pressure is $p=S/c=3.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. The extra factor of c between them converts density to flux.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Momentum density is momentum per volume, not momentum flux.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Divide energy flux by c squared for density.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Divide energy flux by c once for absorbed pressure.

commonErrors.description: Uses S over c for both momentum density and pressure.
commonErrors.consequence: Momentum per volume is confused with momentum flux.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies S by c squared to obtain density.
commonErrors.consequence: The units and magnitude are grossly incorrect.

problems.flawedProof: Both momentum density and pressure equal $S/c=3.00\times10^{-6}$ because they describe the same momentum carried by light.

problems.title: Nodes of an electromagnetic standing wave
problems.objective: Superpose counterpropagating waves and locate electric-field nodes.
problems.statement: Two vacuum waves of equal electric amplitude $E_0$, both polarized along $y$, travel in opposite x directions: $\mathbf E_1=E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\mathbf E_2=E_0\cos(kx+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$. Find the total electric field, the total magnetic field, and the locations of electric nodes.
permittedResults: Trigonometric sum identities and the vacuum plane-wave field relation.
problems.strategy: First: Add the electric waves using the cosine sum identity. Next: The magnetic field reverses relative sign when propagation direction reverses. Finally: Electric nodes require $\cos kx=0$ for all time.
hints: Add the electric waves using the cosine sum identity.
The magnetic field reverses relative sign when propagation direction reverses.
Electric nodes require $\cos kx=0$ for all time.
problems.solution: The electric sum is $\mathbf E=2E_0\cos kx\cos\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf y}$. The magnetic fields are $\mathbf B_1=(E_0/c)\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf B_2=-(E_0/c)\cos(kx+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}$, so $\mathbf B=2(E_0/c)\sin kx\sin\omega t\,\hat{\mathbf z}$. Electric nodes occur at $kx=(2n+1)\pi/2$, or $x=(2n+1)\lambda/4$. Electric antinodes coincide with magnetic nodes.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Add the electric waves using the cosine sum identity.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The magnetic field reverses relative sign when propagation direction reverses.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Electric nodes require $\cos kx=0$ for all time.

commonErrors.description: Gives the two magnetic waves the same directional sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting magnetic standing-wave pattern has the wrong nodes and phase.

commonErrors.description: Locates electric nodes where sine kx vanishes.
commonErrors.consequence: Nodes and antinodes are interchanged.

problems.flawedProof: All components add with the same sign, so $\mathbf E=2E_0\sin kx\cos\omega t\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\mathbf B=2E_0\cos kx\cos\omega t\hat{\mathbf z}/c$. Nodes are at $x=n\lambda/2$.

problems.title: Power flow through a coaxial cable
problems.objective: Integrate the Poynting vector in a coaxial line and recover circuit power.
problems.statement: A long ideal coaxial cable has inner radius $a$, outer-conductor inner radius $b$, potential difference $V$, and current $I$ on the inner conductor with return current on the outer conductor. In the dielectric, use $E_r=V/[r\ln(b/a)]$ and $B_\phi=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$. Find the Poynting vector and integrate it across the annulus to show that the transmitted power is $VI$.
problems.strategy: First: Use cylindrical unit-vector orientation to determine the axial direction. Next: The power element is S times the annular area element $2\pi r\,dr$. Finally: The logarithmic radial integral cancels the field normalization.
hints: Use cylindrical unit-vector orientation to determine the axial direction.
The power element is S times the annular area element $2\pi r\,dr$.
The logarithmic radial integral cancels the field normalization.
problems.solution: With signs chosen for power in $+z$, $\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ points along $+z$ and $S_z=VI/[2\pi r^2\ln(b/a)]$. Therefore $P=\int_a^b S_z(2\pi r\,dr)=VI[\ln(b/a)]^{-1}\int_a^b dr/r=VI$. Energy is transported through the dielectric fields, even though the familiar circuit variables are defined on the conductors.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use cylindrical unit-vector orientation to determine the axial direction.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The power element is S times the annular area element $2\pi r\,dr$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The logarithmic radial integral cancels the field normalization.

commonErrors.description: Integrates S with dr rather than the annular area element.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial geometry and units of power are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims all energy flows inside the metal because current flows there.
commonErrors.consequence: The external electromagnetic energy flux is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Since ideal conductors have zero electric field, the Poynting vector is zero everywhere and the cable cannot transmit field energy; $VI$ travels only with the electrons.

problems.title: Radial current required by local charge conservation
problems.objective: Use the continuity equation to determine current through a shrinking charge distribution.
problems.statement: Inside a sphere of radius $R=0.100\,\mathrm m$, the charge density is spatially uniform and decreases at $\partial\rho/\partial t=-4.00\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$. Assume spherical symmetry. Find the radial current density at the surface, including its direction.
permittedResults: $\partial\rho/\partial t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$ and its volume-integral form.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate the continuity equation over the sphere. Next: Spherical symmetry makes the surface current density uniform and radial. Finally: A decreasing enclosed positive charge requires outward conventional current.
hints: Integrate the continuity equation over the sphere.
Spherical symmetry makes the surface current density uniform and radial.
A decreasing enclosed positive charge requires outward conventional current.
problems.solution: Integrating gives $\oint\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf A=-\int(\partial\rho/\partial t)dV=(4.00)(4\pi R^3/3)$. Since $\mathbf J=J_r\hat{\mathbf r}$ at the surface, $J_r4\pi R^2=(4.00)(4\pi R^3/3)$, hence $J_r=4R/3=0.133\,\mathrm{A/m^2}$ outward.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Integrate the continuity equation over the sphere.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Spherical symmetry makes the surface current density uniform and radial.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: A decreasing enclosed positive charge requires outward conventional current.

commonErrors.description: Assigns inward current because the density derivative is negative.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical direction of charge leaving the volume is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses sphere volume instead of area when solving for current density.
commonErrors.consequence: The result has the wrong dimensions.

problems.flawedProof: Because $\partial\rho/\partial t<0$, current density is $-4.00\hat{\mathbf r}\,\mathrm{A/m^2}$ everywhere; no integration is needed.

problems.title: Deriving the vacuum electromagnetic wave equation
problems.objective: Derive the electric and magnetic wave equations from source-free Maxwell equations.
problems.statement: In a vacuum region with $\rho=0$ and $\mathbf J=0$, derive the wave equations for $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ from Maxwell's equations. Identify the wave speed. State exactly where the divergence equations enter the derivation.
problems.strategy: First: Take the curl of Faraday's law for the electric-field equation. Next: Use the source-free divergence equation to remove the gradient-divergence term. Finally: Repeat with Ampere-Maxwell law and compare with the standard wave equation.
hints: Take the curl of Faraday's law for the electric-field equation.
Use the source-free divergence equation to remove the gradient-divergence term.
Repeat with Ampere-Maxwell law and compare with the standard wave equation.
problems.solution:
Taking the curl of $
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$ gives $
abla(
abla\cdot\mathbf E)-
abla^2\mathbf E=-\partial_t(
abla	imes\mathbf B)$. In vacuum, $
abla\cdot\mathbf E=0$ and $
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$, so $
abla^2\mathbf E=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2\mathbf E$. Similarly, curling Ampere-Maxwell law and using $
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ and Faraday's law gives $
abla^2\mathbf B=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2\mathbf B$. Both propagate at $v=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}=c$. The divergence equations are what eliminate longitudinal source terms in this source-free region.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Take the curl of Faraday's law for the electric-field equation.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use the source-free divergence equation to remove the gradient-divergence term.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Repeat with Ampere-Maxwell law and compare with the standard wave equation.

commonErrors.description: Drops the gradient-divergence term without invoking a divergence equation.
commonErrors.consequence: A necessary source-free step is hidden and would fail in a charged region.

commonErrors.description: Loses one minus sign when combining the two curl equations.
commonErrors.consequence: The result becomes an elliptic rather than propagating wave equation.

problems.flawedProof: Curling Faraday's law gives $\nabla^2\mathbf E=-\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2\mathbf E$ because curl curl always equals Laplacian. Therefore the fields decay rather than propagate.

problems.title: Rotation of a quadrature-polarized wave
problems.objective: Analyze constant-magnitude polarization and its time rotation without relying on ambiguous handedness labels.
problems.statement: A wave traveling in $+z$ has $\mathbf E(z,t)=E_0[\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}]$. Show that its electric-field magnitude is constant. At $z=0$, state the field direction at $t=0$, $t=T/4$, $t=T/2$, and $t=3T/4$.
problems.strategy: First: Square and add the orthogonal field components. Next: At z equals zero, the phase is minus omega t. Finally: Evaluate the two trigonometric components at quarter-period steps.
hints: Square and add the orthogonal field components.
At z equals zero, the phase is minus omega t.
Evaluate the two trigonometric components at quarter-period steps.
problems.solution: The magnitude satisfies $|\mathbf E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\phi+\sin^2\phi)=E_0^2$, so the tip traces a circle. At $z=0$: $t=0$ gives $+E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$; $t=T/4$ gives $-E_0\hat{\mathbf y}$; $t=T/2$ gives $-E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$; and $t=3T/4$ gives $+E_0\hat{\mathbf y}$. This explicit sequence is convention-safe; a handedness name additionally requires a specified viewing convention.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Square and add the orthogonal field components.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: At z equals zero, the phase is minus omega t.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Evaluate the two trigonometric components at quarter-period steps.

commonErrors.description: Adds the component magnitudes rather than adding their squares.
commonErrors.consequence: The field magnitude is incorrectly made time dependent.

commonErrors.description: Uses positive omega t at z equals zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The rotation sequence is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: The magnitude is $E_0(\cos\phi+\sin\phi)$, so the wave alternates between linear and circular polarization. At quarter period it points in $+y$.

problems.title: Normal-incidence reflection at a dielectric boundary
problems.objective: Calculate field amplitudes and power fractions across a lossless interface.
problems.statement: A plane wave in vacuum is normally incident on a lossless, nonmagnetic dielectric with refractive index $n_2=2.00$. The incident electric amplitude is $120\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Find the reflected and transmitted electric amplitudes, including the reflected sign, and the reflected and transmitted power fractions.
permittedResults: At normal incidence $r=(\eta_2-\eta_1)/(\eta_2+\eta_1)$, $t=1+r$, and $\eta=Z_0/n$ for nonmagnetic media.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\eta_2=\eta_1/2$ before evaluating the amplitude coefficients. Next: The negative reflection coefficient represents a pi phase reversal. Finally: Use $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(\eta_1/\eta_2)|t|^2$.
hints: Use $\eta_2=\eta_1/2$ before evaluating the amplitude coefficients.
The negative reflection coefficient represents a pi phase reversal.
Use $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(\eta_1/\eta_2)|t|^2$.
problems.solution: Since $\eta_2=\eta_1/2$, $r=(1/2-1)/(1/2+1)=-1/3$ and $t=2/3$. Thus $E_{r0}=-40.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $E_{t0}=80.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$. The power fractions are $R=r^2=1/9$ and $T=(\eta_1/\eta_2)t^2=2(4/9)=8/9$. Their sum is one, as required for a lossless boundary.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $\eta_2=\eta_1/2$ before evaluating the amplitude coefficients.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The negative reflection coefficient represents a pi phase reversal.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Use $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(\eta_1/\eta_2)|t|^2$.

commonErrors.description: Uses refractive index directly in place of impedance without inversion.
commonErrors.consequence: The reflection phase and amplitudes are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets the transmitted power fraction equal to t squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The change in wave impedance is omitted and energy appears not to be conserved.

problems.flawedProof: Because the transmitted field is $2/3$ of the incident field, $T=4/9$. The remaining $5/9$ must be reflected, so $E_{r0}=+89.4\,\mathrm{V/m}$.

problems.title: Skin depth and attenuation in copper
problems.objective: Estimate field penetration into a good conductor at radio frequency.
problems.statement: Treat copper as a good conductor with $\sigma=5.80\times10^7\,\mathrm{S/m}$ and $\mu=\mu_0$. At $f=1.00\,\mathrm{MHz}$, find the skin depth. What fraction of the surface electric-field amplitude remains at depth $0.200\,\mathrm{mm}$?
permittedResults: For a good conductor, $\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)}$ and field amplitude varies as $e^{-z/\delta}$.
problems.strategy: First: Convert frequency to angular frequency with $\omega=2\pi f$. Next: Keep meters consistent when comparing depth with skin depth. Finally: The requested fraction is an amplitude ratio, not an intensity ratio.
hints: Convert frequency to angular frequency with $\omega=2\pi f$.
Keep meters consistent when comparing depth with skin depth.
The requested fraction is an amplitude ratio, not an intensity ratio.
problems.solution: The skin depth is $\delta=\sqrt{2/[\mu_0\sigma(2\pi f)]}=6.61\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm m=66.1\,\mu\mathrm m$. The depth is $z/\delta=(2.00\times10^{-4})/(6.61\times10^{-5})=3.03$, so the amplitude fraction is $e^{-3.03}=4.84\times10^{-2}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Convert frequency to angular frequency with $\omega=2\pi f$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Keep meters consistent when comparing depth with skin depth.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The requested fraction is an amplitude ratio, not an intensity ratio.

commonErrors.description: Uses frequency f where angular frequency omega is required.
commonErrors.consequence: The skin depth is too large by the square root of two pi.

commonErrors.description: Uses exp minus two z over delta for the field amplitude.
commonErrors.consequence: An intensity attenuation law is substituted for amplitude attenuation.

problems.flawedProof: The skin depth is $2/(\mu_0\sigma f)=2.74\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm m$, and the amplitude fraction is $e^{-2z/\delta}$.

problems.title: Low-loss propagation in a weakly conducting dielectric
problems.objective: Evaluate loss tangent, attenuation, and phase constant in a weakly conducting medium.
problems.statement: A nonmagnetic material at $1.00\,\mathrm{GHz}$ has $\epsilon_r=4.00$ and conductivity $\sigma=2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{S/m}$. Compute its loss tangent. Using the low-loss approximations $\alpha\approx(\sigma/2)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ and $\beta\approx\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$, find $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the electric-amplitude fraction after $1.00\,\mathrm m$.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\epsilon=4\epsilon_0$ and $\omega=2\pi\times10^9\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Next: Recognize $\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}=Z_0/2$ for this nonmagnetic material. Finally: The amplitude varies as $e^{-\alpha z}$.
hints: Use $\epsilon=4\epsilon_0$ and $\omega=2\pi\times10^9\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Recognize $\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}=Z_0/2$ for this nonmagnetic material.
The amplitude varies as $e^{-\alpha z}$.
problems.solution: The loss tangent is $\sigma/(\omega\epsilon)=0.0200/[2\pi(10^9)(4\epsilon_0)]=8.99\times10^{-2}$, small enough for a leading low-loss estimate. The medium impedance factor is $\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}=Z_0/2=188.4\,\Omega$, so $\alpha\approx(0.0200/2)(188.4)=1.88\,\mathrm{Np/m}$. Also $\beta\approx\omega/(c/2)=41.9\,\mathrm{rad/m}$. After one meter, $E/E_0=e^{-1.88}=0.152$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use $\epsilon=4\epsilon_0$ and $\omega=2\pi\times10^9\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Recognize $\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}=Z_0/2$ for this nonmagnetic material.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: The amplitude varies as $e^{-\alpha z}$.

commonErrors.description: Treats loss tangent as sigma times omega epsilon.
commonErrors.consequence: The dimensionless comparison of conduction and displacement current is inverted.

commonErrors.description: Uses exp minus beta z for attenuation.
commonErrors.consequence: Phase accumulation is confused with amplitude decay.

problems.flawedProof: Because $\beta$ is larger than $\alpha$, the amplitude fraction is $e^{-\beta}=6.5\times10^{-19}$. The loss tangent is $\sigma\omega\epsilon$.

problems.title: Fundamental mode between conducting planes
problems.objective: Apply conducting boundary conditions to a one-dimensional electromagnetic cavity mode.
problems.statement: Two perfectly conducting planes are at $x=0$ and $x=L$. A source-free cavity field has the form $\mathbf E=E_0\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$. Determine the allowed k values, derive the corresponding frequencies, and find the fundamental frequency for $L=0.150\,\mathrm m$.
permittedResults: Tangential electric field vanishes at a perfect conductor and vacuum fields obey the wave equation.
problems.strategy: First: The field already vanishes at x equals zero; impose the second boundary at x equals L. Next: Use $\sin(kL)=0$ to quantize k. Finally: Relate angular frequency and wave number by $\omega=ck$.
hints: The field already vanishes at x equals zero; impose the second boundary at x equals L.
Use $\sin(kL)=0$ to quantize k.
Relate angular frequency and wave number by $\omega=ck$.
problems.solution: The boundary at $x=L$ requires $\sin(kL)=0$, hence $k_n=n\pi/L$ for positive integers n. The vacuum dispersion relation gives $\omega_n=ck_n$ and $f_n=nc/(2L)$. For $L=0.150\,\mathrm m$, $f_1=c/(0.300\,\mathrm m)=9.99\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$, approximately $1.00\,\mathrm{GHz}$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The field already vanishes at x equals zero; impose the second boundary at x equals L.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $\sin(kL)=0$ to quantize k.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Relate angular frequency and wave number by $\omega=ck$.

commonErrors.description: Allows n equals zero as a nonzero electromagnetic mode.
commonErrors.consequence: The field is identically zero but is counted as a resonance.

commonErrors.description: Uses kL equal to pi over two at the second conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: An electric antinode is placed where tangential electric field must vanish.

problems.flawedProof: The field should be largest at both metal surfaces, so $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/L$ and the fundamental frequency is $c/(4L)$.

problems.title: Normalizing the dipole radiation pattern
problems.objective: Normalize the angular power distribution of an ideal oscillating dipole.
problems.statement: An ideal electric dipole radiates total time-averaged power $P=12.0\,\mathrm W$ with angular distribution $dP/d\Omega=A\sin^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is measured from the dipole axis. Determine A, the maximum power per solid angle, and the power per solid angle on the dipole axis.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate the angular distribution over the full sphere. Next: Use $\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta=4/3$. Finally: Evaluate the normalized pattern at the equator and axis.
hints: Integrate the angular distribution over the full sphere.
Use $\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta=4/3$.
Evaluate the normalized pattern at the equator and axis.
problems.solution: The total power is $P=A\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta=A(2\pi)(4/3)=8\pi A/3$. Thus $A=3P/(8\pi)=1.43\,\mathrm{W/sr}$. The maximum occurs at $\theta=\pi/2$ and equals A. On the dipole axis, $\sin^2\theta=0$, so $dP/d\Omega=0$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Integrate the angular distribution over the full sphere.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use $\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta=4/3$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Evaluate the normalized pattern at the equator and axis.

commonErrors.description: Integrates sin squared theta only over theta and omits the solid-angle sine factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The normalization constant is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Places maximum radiation on the dipole axis.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining angular pattern is interpreted backward.

problems.flawedProof: The integral of $\sin^2\theta$ from zero to pi is $\pi/2$, so $P=A\pi/2$. Radiation is strongest at theta equals zero because that is the dipole direction.

problems.title: Charging current and the field in a capacitor gap
problems.objective: Reconcile conduction and displacement current while calculating a time-dependent magnetic field.
problems.statement: A circular parallel-plate capacitor of radius $R=6.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ is charged by $I(t)=I_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $I_0=1.20\,\mathrm A$ and $\tau=2.00\,\mathrm{ms}$. Neglect fringing. At $t=1.00\,\mathrm{ms}$, find (a) $dE/dt$ in the gap, (b) B at $r=3.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ in the gap, and (c) B at $r=9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$. Explain why an Ampere-Maxwell loop at $r=9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ gives the same result whether its spanning surface cuts the wire or bows through the gap.
problems.strategy: First: Evaluate the charging current at the specified time before using it elsewhere. Next: Inside the plate radius, only the area fraction r squared over R squared is enclosed. Finally: Outside the plates, both admissible spanning surfaces enclose the same total effective current.
hints: Evaluate the charging current at the specified time before using it elsewhere.
Inside the plate radius, only the area fraction r squared over R squared is enclosed.
Outside the plates, both admissible spanning surfaces enclose the same total effective current.
problems.solution: At $t=1.00\,\mathrm{ms}$, $I=1.20e^{-0.5}=0.728\,\mathrm A$. With $A=\pi(0.0600)^2$, $dE/dt=I/(\epsilon_0A)=7.27\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$. For $r<R$, $B=\mu_0Ir/(2\pi R^2)=1.21\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T$ at $0.0300\,\mathrm m$. For $r>R$, $B=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)=1.62\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T$ at $0.0900\,\mathrm m$. A surface cutting the wire encloses conduction current I; a surface through the gap encloses displacement current $\epsilon_0A\,dE/dt=I$. The Maxwell term therefore removes the surface ambiguity.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Evaluate the charging current at the specified time before using it elsewhere.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Inside the plate radius, only the area fraction r squared over R squared is enclosed.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Outside the plates, both admissible spanning surfaces enclose the same total effective current.

commonErrors.description: Uses the initial current instead of evaluating the exponential at one millisecond.
commonErrors.consequence: Every numerical field and field-rate result is too large.

commonErrors.description: Declares zero enclosed current for a surface through the capacitor gap.
commonErrors.consequence: The magnetic circulation becomes spuriously dependent on the chosen spanning surface.

problems.flawedProof: The current is still $1.20\,\mathrm A$ because the capacitor is charging. A surface through the gap encloses no current, so it predicts $B=0$ even though a wire-cutting surface predicts a nonzero field; Ampere's law is therefore inconsistent.

problems.title: Deriving Poynting's theorem
problems.objective: Derive local electromagnetic energy conservation and interpret each term.
problems.statement: In a linear vacuum region containing current density $\mathbf J$, derive Poynting's theorem $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ from Faraday's law and Ampere-Maxwell law. Identify u and $\mathbf S$, and interpret the sign of the work term.
permittedResults:
$
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B)=\mathbf B\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf B)$.
problems.strategy: First: Dot E into Ampere-Maxwell law and B over mu-zero into Faraday's law. Next: Use the vector identity to combine the curl terms into a divergence. Finally: Recognize time derivatives of quadratic electric and magnetic energy densities.
hints: Dot E into Ampere-Maxwell law and B over mu-zero into Faraday's law.
Use the vector identity to combine the curl terms into a divergence.
Recognize time derivatives of quadratic electric and magnetic energy densities.
problems.solution:
From $
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$ and $
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$, the vector identity gives $
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B/\mu_0)=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E-(1/\mu_0)\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B$. Hence $\partial_t[\epsilon_0E^2/2+B^2/(2\mu_0)]+
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B/\mu_0)=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$. Thus $u=\epsilon_0E^2/2+B^2/(2\mu_0)$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B/\mu_0$. Positive $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ is power delivered by the field to matter, so it decreases field energy unless replenished by inward flux.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Dot E into Ampere-Maxwell law and B over mu-zero into Faraday's law.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use the vector identity to combine the curl terms into a divergence.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Recognize time derivatives of quadratic electric and magnetic energy densities.

commonErrors.description: Assigns positive J dot E as a source term for field energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy transfer between fields and matter is given the wrong direction.

commonErrors.description: Omits the magnetic energy derivative when applying Faraday's law.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting conservation law is incomplete.

problems.flawedProof: Because $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ is electrical power, it must appear with a plus sign as newly created field energy. The magnetic field does no work, so its energy term can be omitted.

problems.title: Oblique radiation force on a perfect mirror
problems.objective: Resolve photon momentum normal to a mirror and distinguish beam area from footprint area.
problems.statement: A $20.0\,\mathrm W$ collimated beam strikes a perfect mirror at $30.0^\circ$ from the surface normal. The beam cross-sectional area perpendicular to propagation is $5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Find the normal force on the mirror and the average normal pressure over the illuminated footprint.
permittedResults: A photon has momentum U over c; specular reflection reverses its normal momentum component.
problems.strategy: First: The normal momentum change is twice the incident normal component. Next: The illuminated mirror footprint is larger than the perpendicular beam area by one over cosine theta. Finally: Divide the normal force by the footprint, not by the beam cross section.
hints: The normal momentum change is twice the incident normal component.
The illuminated mirror footprint is larger than the perpendicular beam area by one over cosine theta.
Divide the normal force by the footprint, not by the beam cross section.
problems.solution: The incident momentum rate is $P/c$, and reflection changes its normal component by $2(P/c)\cos\theta$. Thus $F_n=2(20.0)\cos30^\circ/c=1.16\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm N$. The footprint is $A_f=A_\perp/\cos30^\circ=5.77\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, so $p_n=F_n/A_f=2.00\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. Equivalently, $p_n=2I\cos^2\theta/c$ with $I=P/A_\perp$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: The normal momentum change is twice the incident normal component.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: The illuminated mirror footprint is larger than the perpendicular beam area by one over cosine theta.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Divide the normal force by the footprint, not by the beam cross section.

commonErrors.description: Uses twice P over c without resolving the incident momentum normal to the mirror.
commonErrors.consequence: The force is too large at oblique incidence.

commonErrors.description: Divides by the perpendicular beam cross section rather than the mirror footprint.
commonErrors.consequence: The pressure misses an additional cosine factor.

problems.flawedProof: A perfect mirror always feels $2P/c$, independent of angle. The pressure is that force divided by the beam cross section because projection does not change area.

problems.title: Radiation force with partial reflection and absorption
problems.objective: Account separately for absorbed and reflected momentum at an opaque surface.
problems.statement: A normally incident $100\,\mathrm W$ beam hits an opaque surface with power reflectivity $R=0.700$ and absorptivity $A=0.300$. Find the average radiation force and the absorbed heating power. Assume specular reflection and no transmission.
permittedResults: Absorption transfers P over c and reflection transfers 2P over c for the corresponding power fractions.
problems.strategy: First: Weight the absorption and reflection momentum transfers separately. Next: Use A plus R equals one only after writing the physical contributions. Finally: Heating comes from absorbed power, not reflected power.
hints: Weight the absorption and reflection momentum transfers separately.
Use A plus R equals one only after writing the physical contributions.
Heating comes from absorbed power, not reflected power.
problems.solution: The force is $F=(AP+2RP)/c=(0.300+1.400)(100)/c=5.67\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm N$. Since $A+R=1$, this can also be written $(1+R)P/c$. The heating power is $P_{\rm abs}=AP=30.0\,\mathrm W$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Weight the absorption and reflection momentum transfers separately.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Use A plus R equals one only after writing the physical contributions.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Heating comes from absorbed power, not reflected power.

commonErrors.description: Uses the total incident power in both the absorption and reflection terms.
commonErrors.consequence: The same energy fraction is counted twice.

commonErrors.description: Treats reflected power as heating the target.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy that leaves in the reflected beam is incorrectly deposited.

problems.flawedProof: The surface is opaque, so all $100\,\mathrm W$ becomes heat. Reflection also doubles all incident momentum, giving $F=2P/c$.

problems.title: Phase and group speed in a plasma-like dispersion relation
problems.objective: Differentiate a dispersion relation and interpret superluminal phase speed safely.
problems.statement: A wave obeys $\omega^2=\omega_p^2+c^2k^2$. At $k=2\omega_p/c$, find the phase speed $v_p=\omega/k$ and group speed $v_g=d\omega/dk$. Show their product and explain why $v_p>c$ does not by itself imply superluminal signal transport.
permittedResults: Definitions of phase and group velocity and elementary differentiation.
problems.strategy: First: Evaluate omega from the dispersion relation at the specified k. Next: Differentiate the positive-frequency branch with respect to k. Finally: Distinguish motion of a constant phase from motion of an envelope or information.
hints: Evaluate omega from the dispersion relation at the specified k.
Differentiate the positive-frequency branch with respect to k.
Distinguish motion of a constant phase from motion of an envelope or information.
problems.solution: At the given k, $\omega=\sqrt5\,\omega_p$. Hence $v_p=\omega/k=(\sqrt5/2)c=1.118c$. Differentiation gives $v_g=c^2k/\omega=(2/\sqrt5)c=0.894c$, so $v_pv_g=c^2$. A phase crest is not a localized signal or energy packet; the group speed here is subluminal and is the relevant envelope speed within the model.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Evaluate omega from the dispersion relation at the specified k.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate the positive-frequency branch with respect to k.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Distinguish motion of a constant phase from motion of an envelope or information.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates omega squared but forgets the factor 2 omega.
commonErrors.consequence: The group velocity has the wrong dimensions or magnitude.

commonErrors.description: Identifies phase speed directly with information speed.
commonErrors.consequence: A superluminal signaling claim is made from the wrong velocity concept.

problems.flawedProof: Since $v_p=1.118c$, the wave carries information faster than light. Differentiating gives $v_g=2c^2k$, which is even faster.

problems.title: Deriving electromagnetic interface conditions
problems.objective: Derive the four macroscopic Maxwell boundary conditions from integral laws.
problems.statement: An interface carries free surface charge density $\sigma_f$ and free surface current density $\mathbf K_f$, with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ pointing from medium 1 to medium 2. Derive the boundary conditions for the normal components of $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ and the tangential components of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$. Assume finite nonsingular fields and explain which infinitesimal Gaussian surfaces or loops are used.
permittedResults: The macroscopic integral Maxwell equations and standard limiting pillbox and loop arguments.
problems.strategy: First: Use thin pillboxes for the two divergence laws. Next: Use narrow rectangular loops for Faraday and Ampere-Maxwell laws. Finally: Track the chosen normal orientation when writing each vector jump.

problems.solution: A pillbox crossing the interface gives $\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f$ from Gauss's electric law and $\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf B_2-\mathbf B_1)=0$ from Gauss's magnetic law. Ampere-Maxwell law on the analogous loop leaves the enclosed surface current while the finite displacement-flux term vanishes, giving $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_f$. These are statements about free surface sources when D and H are used.

problems.title: Complete plane-wave reconstruction in a dielectric
problems.objective: Reconstruct all wave parameters and verify Ampere-Maxwell law from intensity and material data.
problems.statement: A sinusoidal plane wave of frequency $60.0\,\mathrm{MHz}$ travels in $+z$ through a lossless medium with $\epsilon_r=9.00$ and $\mu_r=1.00$. Its average intensity is $12.0\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ and $\mathbf E$ is polarized along $+x$. Find the phase speed, wavelength, intrinsic impedance, peak $E$, $H$, and $B$ amplitudes, and peak displacement-current density. Write consistent field expressions and verify their amplitudes satisfy Ampere-Maxwell law.

Choose B along positive y so that E cross H points in positive z.

The peak displacement-current density is $J_{d0}=\omega\epsilon E_0=1.65\,\mathrm{A/m^2}$. Numerically, $kB_0=2.07\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T/m}=\mu_0J_{d0}$, verifying the curl-amplitude relation.

problems.title: Quarter-wave antireflection coating
problems.objective: Derive the refractive index and thickness that cancel reflection from a single dielectric layer.
problems.statement: At normal incidence, air $(n_1=1.00)$ borders a lossless coating of index $n_2$, followed by glass $(n_3=1.50)$. For nonmagnetic media use $r_{ij}=(n_i-n_j)/(n_i+n_j)$ and the layer reflection coefficient $r=(r_{12}+r_{23}e^{2i\beta})/(1+r_{12}r_{23}e^{2i\beta})$, where $\beta=2\pi n_2d/\lambda_0$. Find $n_2$ and the smallest positive thickness d that make reflection vanish at vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0=600\,\mathrm{nm}$.
permittedResults: The stated exact single-layer reflection coefficient.
problems.strategy: First: Choose a quarter-wave optical thickness so the round-trip layer phase contributes a minus sign. Next: Then require the two interface reflection coefficients to be equal. Finally: Solve $n_2^2=n_1n_3$ and $n_2d=\lambda_0/4$.
hints: Choose a quarter-wave optical thickness so the round-trip layer phase contributes a minus sign.
Then require the two interface reflection coefficients to be equal.
Solve $n_2^2=n_1n_3$ and $n_2d=\lambda_0/4$.
problems.solution: The smallest destructive round-trip phase has $\beta=\pi/2$, so $e^{2i\beta}=-1$ and the numerator becomes $r_{12}-r_{23}$. Setting it to zero gives $(n_1-n_2)/(n_1+n_2)=(n_2-n_3)/(n_2+n_3)$, which simplifies to $n_2^2=n_1n_3$. Thus $n_2=\sqrt{1.50}=1.225$. The quarter-wave thickness is $d=\lambda_0/(4n_2)=600\,\mathrm{nm}/(4\times1.225)=122\,\mathrm{nm}$. The denominator remains nonzero, so the total reflected amplitude vanishes at the design wavelength.

problems.title: Brewster incidence and the surviving s reflection
problems.objective: Apply oblique-incidence geometry to compare p and s polarized reflection.
problems.statement: Light travels from air $(n_1=1.00)$ to glass $(n_2=1.50)$ at the Brewster angle. Find the incident and transmitted angles. problems.strategy: First: At Brewster incidence, the refracted and reflected rays are perpendicular. Next: Use Snell's law to confirm the transmitted angle. Finally: Square the real s-amplitude coefficient to obtain its power reflectance.

Use Snell's law to confirm the transmitted angle.
Square the real s-amplitude coefficient to obtain its power reflectance.

problems.title: Mode selection and velocities in a rectangular waveguide

problems.title: Energy, loss, linewidth, and ringdown of a cavity

Using $Q=\omega_0U/P_{\rm loss}$, find the average dissipated power, the full-width resonance linewidth $\Delta f=f_0/Q$, the energy-decay time constant, and the field-amplitude decay time constant after the drive is removed.

Solve the first-order energy decay equation for its time constant.
Because energy is quadratic in field amplitude, the amplitude time constant is twice the energy time constant.

problems.title: Poynting flow into a charging capacitor
problems.objective: Show that field energy enters a capacitor through its lateral surface at the circuit power rate.
problems.statement: A circular parallel-plate capacitor has plate radius R, separation d, negligible fringing, voltage V, and charging current I. Between the plates take $E=V/d$ and use Ampere-Maxwell law to find B at the plate edge. Show that the inward Poynting flux through the cylindrical side surface equals $VI=dU/dt$. State the direction of $\mathbf S$.
permittedResults: $\mathbf S=(1/\mu_0)\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and Ampere-Maxwell law.
problems.strategy: First: At the plate edge, the enclosed displacement current equals I, so $B=\mu_0I/(2\pi R)$. Next: Use the cylindrical side area two pi R d rather than the plate area. Finally: Check the cross-product direction for axial E and azimuthal B.

Use the cylindrical side area two pi R d rather than the plate area.

Since circuit power into the capacitor is $VI$, this equals $dU/dt$.

Using $E_r=Q/(2\pi\epsilon_0Lr)$ and $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$, find the total electromagnetic angular momentum about the z axis, including its direction.

problems.title: Magnetic-dielectric interface with exact energy accounting
problems.objective: Derive normal-incidence coefficients for magnetic media and verify power conservation numerically.
problems.statement: A $120\,\mathrm{MHz}$ plane wave is normally incident from lossless medium 1 with $(\epsilon_{r1},\mu_{r1})=(4.00,1.00)$ onto lossless medium 2 with $(\epsilon_{r2},\mu_{r2})=(2.25,4.00)$. The incident peak electric amplitude is $55.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Starting from tangential E and H continuity, derive the electric reflection and transmission coefficients, carefully accounting for the reflected H direction. Then find reflected and transmitted field amplitudes, power fractions, average power fluxes, and wavelengths in both media. Verify energy conservation.
problems.strategy: First: Write $E_i+E_r=E_t$ but $E_i/\eta_1-E_r/\eta_1=E_t/\eta_2$. Next: Solve before substituting the two impedances, then use impedance-weighted power transmission. Finally: Use each medium's phase speed for its wavelength while keeping frequency continuous.
hints: Write $E_i+E_r=E_t$ but $E_i/\eta_1-E_r/\eta_1=E_t/\eta_2$.
Solve before substituting the two impedances, then use impedance-weighted power transmission.
Use each medium's phase speed for its wavelength while keeping frequency continuous.
problems.solution: The boundary equations give $r=E_r/E_i=(\eta_2-\eta_1)/(\eta_2+\eta_1)$ and $t=E_t/E_i=2\eta_2/(\eta_2+\eta_1)=1+r$. Here $\eta_1=Z_0/2$ and $\eta_2=4Z_0/3$, so $r=5/11$ and $t=16/11$. Thus $E_{r0}=25.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $E_{t0}=80.0\,\mathrm{V/m}$. The power fractions are $R=r^2=25/121$ and $T=(\eta_1/\eta_2)t^2=96/121$, so $R+T=1$. The incident flux is $E_{i0}^2/(2\eta_1)=8.03\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$; reflected and transmitted magnitudes are $1.66$ and $6.37\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$, which sum to the incident value within rounding. The speeds are $c/2$ and $c/3$, giving $\lambda_1=1.25\,\mathrm m$ and $\lambda_2=0.833\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Gaussian wave-packet broadening from group dispersion
problems.objective: Derive the evolving envelope of a narrowband Gaussian packet under quadratic dispersion.
problems.statement: A one-dimensional narrowband packet has initial complex envelope $A(z,0)=A_0e^{-z^2/(2L_0^2)}$. Near carrier wave number $k_0$, let $\omega(k_0+q)=\omega_0+v_gq+\tfrac12Dq^2$, with real constant $D=d^2\omega/dk^2$. Fourier-evolve the envelope to show how its center, width parameter, and peak magnitude change. Then evaluate the width factor and peak-amplitude factor at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$ for $L_0=2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m$ and $D=3.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
permittedResults: The Fourier transform of a Gaussian and the standard complex Gaussian integral.
problems.strategy: First: After removing the carrier, integrate $e^{-L_0^2q^2/2+iq(z-v_gt)-iDq^2t/2}$ over q. Next: Combine the quadratic terms into the complex width $L_0^2+iDt$. Finally: Take the modulus to separate translation, broadening, and peak reduction.
hints: After removing the carrier, integrate $e^{-L_0^2q^2/2+iq(z-v_gt)-iDq^2t/2}$ over q.
Combine the quadratic terms into the complex width $L_0^2+iDt$.
Take the modulus to separate translation, broadening, and peak reduction.
problems.solution: Gaussian integration gives, up to the carrier phase, $A(z,t)=A_0L_0(L_0^2+iDt)^{-1/2}\exp[-(z-v_gt)^2/(2(L_0^2+iDt))]$. The center moves at $v_g$. The modulus has Gaussian width parameter $L(t)=L_0\sqrt{1+(Dt/L_0^2)^2}$, while the peak magnitude is reduced by $[1+(Dt/L_0^2)^2]^{-1/4}$; their combination preserves integrated packet energy in this lossless model. Numerically, $Dt/L_0^2=(3.00\times10^{-4})(2.00)/(4.00\times10^{-4})=1.50$. Thus the width factor is $\sqrt{3.25}=1.80$, so $L=3.61\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m$, and the peak-amplitude factor is $3.25^{-1/4}=0.745$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: After removing the carrier, integrate $e^{-L_0^2q^2/2+iq(z-v_gt)-iDq^2t/2}$ over q.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Combine the quadratic terms into the complex width $L_0^2+iDt$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Take the modulus to separate translation, broadening, and peak reduction.

problems.title: Maxwell waves in a conducting material
problems.objective: Derive exact propagation and attenuation in a linear conductor and connect it to local energy loss.
problems.statement: A homogeneous isotropic material has constants $\epsilon$, $\mu$, and conductivity $\sigma$, with $\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E$ and no free charge accumulation. Using fields proportional to $e^{i(kz-\omega t)}$, derive the complex dispersion relation for a transverse electromagnetic wave. Write $k=\beta+i\alpha$ so amplitude decays in $+z$, derive exact formulas for $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and recover the low-loss and good-conductor limits. Use Poynting's theorem to identify the local loss. Finally, for $\epsilon_r=4.00$, $\mu_r=1.00$, $\sigma=0.100\,\mathrm{S/m}$, and $f=100\,\mathrm{MHz}$, find the loss tangent, $\alpha$, $\beta$, the $1/e$ amplitude depth, and wavelength.
permittedResults: Maxwell equations in a linear medium, Poynting's theorem, and algebra for a complex square root.
problems.strategy: First: Use Faraday to express B through $\mathbf k\times\mathbf E$, then substitute into Ampere-Maxwell with $\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E$. Next: Equate real and imaginary parts of $(\beta+i\alpha)^2=\mu\epsilon\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$. Finally: Check the asymptotic regimes using $x=\sigma/(\omega\epsilon)$, then use $-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ in the energy balance.
hints: Use Faraday to express B through $\mathbf k\times\mathbf E$, then substitute into Ampere-Maxwell with $\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E$.
Equate real and imaginary parts of $(\beta+i\alpha)^2=\mu\epsilon\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$.
Check the asymptotic regimes using $x=\sigma/(\omega\epsilon)$, then use $-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ in the energy balance.
problems.solution:
For transverse E, Faraday gives $\mathbf B=(1/\omega)\mathbf k\times\mathbf E$. Substitution in $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\sigma\mathbf E+\partial_t(\epsilon\mathbf E)$ yields $k^2=\mu\epsilon\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$. With $k=\beta+i\alpha$, $\beta^2-\alpha^2=\mu\epsilon\omega^2$ and $2\alpha\beta=\mu\sigma\omega$. Defining $x=\sigma/(\omega\epsilon)$ gives
$\alpha=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon/2}\,[\sqrt{1+x^2}-1]^{1/2}$ and $\beta=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon/2}\,[\sqrt{1+x^2}+1]^{1/2}$.
For $x\ll1$, $\alpha\approx(\sigma/2)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ and $\beta\approx\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$. For $x\gg1$, $\alpha\approx\beta\approx\sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma/2}$. Time-averaged Poynting balance is $\nabla\cdot\langle\mathbf S\rangle=-\langle\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\rangle=-\sigma|E_0|^2/2$, so declining flux becomes Joule heat. Numerically, $x=4.49$, $\alpha=5.63\,\mathrm{Np/m}$, and $\beta=7.02\,\mathrm{rad/m}$. The amplitude depth is $1/\alpha=0.178\,\mathrm m$ and $\lambda=2\pi/\beta=0.896\,\mathrm m$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses and states the correct physical setup: Use Faraday to express B through $\mathbf k\times\mathbf E$, then substitute into Ampere-Maxwell with $\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E$.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Equate real and imaginary parts of $(\beta+i\alpha)^2=\mu\epsilon\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Check the asymptotic regimes using $x=\sigma/(\omega\epsilon)$, then use $-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ in the energy balance.
